title: Female Team-Sport Athletes' Physical Fitness and Jump Performance Kinematics After Plyometric Jump Training: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Plyometric jump training (PJT) can improve athletes' physical fitness across a range of sports and populations. Nonetheless, the role of PJT in adult female team-sport athletes' fitness, jump performance, and kinematics remains unclear, particularly given the increasing number of published, heterogeneous studies.
OBJECTIVES: This systematic review aimed to first examine the effectiveness of PJT in improving physical fitness and jump-performance kinematics in adult female team-sport athletes, and second, to provide evidence-based recommendations for PJT prescription for this population.
METHODS: A systematic literature search was conducted in the PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and EBSCO databases up to March 2026. The included studies recruited healthy female team-sport athletes (mean age: ≥ 18 years), incorporated a PJT programme ≥ 2 weeks in duration, included comparator groups, and assessed athletes' physical fitness, jump performance, and/or kinematics. The risk of bias (RoB) was assessed using the Physiotherapy Evidence Database scale. Hedges' g effect sizes (ES) with 95% confidence intervals (95% CIs) were reported using a random-effects model for meta-analyses. Statistical significance was set at p ≤ 0.05. Subgroup analyses were conducted based on the participant characteristics (height, body mass, sport) and PJT programming variables (duration, frequency, total sessions, weekly total jumps). The certainty of evidence was assessed using GRADE.
RESULTS: Thirty-one articles were included (n = 609 participants), and 25 were meta-analysed. Two studies were categorised with high RoB (≤ 3 points), 20 studies achieved moderate RoB (4-5 points), and 9 studies achieved low RoB (≥ 6 points). Compared to controls, PJT improved countermovement jump (CMJ) height (ES = 0.550, p < 0.001), CMJ peak concentric velocity (ES = 0.623, p = 0.011), drop jump (DJ) reactive strength index (RSI) (ES = 0.926, p = 0.001), DJ height (ES = 0.721, p = 0.002), 10 m sprint time (ES = 0.712, p = 0.032), 20 m sprint time (ES = 0.709, p < 0.001), 30 m sprint time (ES = 1.018, p = 0.001), non-linear (agility) Illinois test time (ES = 1.225, p < 0.001) and T test sprint time (ES = 0.965, p < 0.001). Compared to PJT ≤ 6 weeks, longer interventions favoured DJ RSI (p = 0.008), 10 m sprint time (p = 0.001), and Illinois agility test time (p < 0.001). Impact of heterogeneity (I2) remained low (≤ 0.06%) in five analyses and moderate in the other four analyses (≤ 73.1%). The certainty of evidence was considered low to moderate for the study outcomes. Two studies reported that a total of three participants possibly sustained an injury during PJT.
CONCLUSIONS: Adult female team-sport athletes' fitness, jump performance, and kinematics improved after PJT when compared to the control condition, including CMJ height, CMJ peak concentric velocity, DJ RSI, linear sprint speed, and non-linear (agility) sprint speed. The improvements were particularly notable with longer interventions (≥ 8 weeks).
TRIAL REGISTRATION: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/NERCY.

title: Effect of percutaneous electrolysis combined with exercise on pain and function in chronic lateral epicondylitis: A randomized controlled trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Percutaneous electrolysis (PE) is a minimally invasive, ultrasound-guided treatment, but its added benefit alongside exercise for chronic lateral epicondylitis remains unclear.
OBJECTIVE: To compare exercise plus PE with exercise alone for pain and function.
DESIGN: Prospective randomized controlled trial.
METHODS: In an outpatient rehabilitation clinic, 68 participants were randomized to exercise plus PE (n = 34) or exercise alone (n = 34). Both groups performed a 2-week home-based stretching and strengthening program; PE was administered on days 1, 8, and 14. The primary outcome was pain intensity on a 0-10 visual analog scale (VAS); secondary outcomes were Patient-Rated Tennis Elbow Evaluation (PRTEE) total score, pressure pain threshold (PPT), and Quick Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand (Q-DASH) score. Assessments occurred at baseline and 1 week, 1 month, and 3 months after treatment completion.
RESULTS: Group-by-time interactions were significant for all outcomes (all p < 0.001). At 3 months, model-estimated between-group mean differences favored PE for VAS (-3.30 points; 95% CI, -3.97 to -2.63) and PRTEE (-20.78 points; 95% CI, -25.98 to -15.57), both p < 0.001. Secondary outcomes favored PE at all follow-ups. In a post hoc exploratory responder analysis, clinically meaningful PRTEE improvement occurred in 79.4% of the PE group versus 2.9% of controls (p < 0.001). No serious adverse events or intervention-related discontinuations occurred.
CONCLUSIONS: Adding ultrasound-guided PE to the tested 2-week home exercise program was associated with greater improvements in pain and function than exercise alone over the 3-month follow-up. Longer-term effects and applicability to other rehabilitation programs remain uncertain.

title: No Differences in Patient-reported Outcomes Between the Direct Anterior and Posterolateral Approach for THA: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The direct anterior approach (DAA) for THA is seeing wider use because it is purported to deliver a faster postoperative recovery. However, most previous studies comparing the DAA with the posterolateral approach (PLA) were limited by small sample sizes, heterogeneous patient populations, and the use of outcome measures with ceiling effects.
QUESTIONS/PURPOSES: (1) Does the DAA result in a higher proportion of patients achieving the patient acceptable symptom state (PASS) on the Hip Disability and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (HOOS) after THA compared with the PLA? (2) Are there differences in symptoms, physical function, life activities and participation, health-related quality of life (QoL), or complications between the DAA and PLA in the first postoperative year?
METHODS: A prospective, parallel-group, nonblinded, randomized controlled trial comparing the DAA and PLA for THA was conducted. Patients with primary or secondary osteoarthritis with an indication for THA with an uncemented femoral stem and cemented acetabular component were eligible. Of the 241 patients assessed for eligibility, 53% (128) were included in the study. Fifty-one percent (65 of 128) were randomized to the DAA group, and 49% (63 of 128) were randomized to the PLA group. One patient in each group was lost to follow-up, leaving 98% (64 of 65) and 98% (62 of 63) of patients available for analysis, respectively. There were no between-group differences in baseline or perioperative measurements. The primary outcome was achievement of the PASS on the HOOS at 3 months postoperatively. An a priori sample-size calculation indicated that 60 patients per group were required to detect a 20% difference in PASS achievement between groups (80% power; α = 0.05). With an expected loss to follow-up of 10%, the sample size was set to 65 patients per group. Secondary outcomes included symptoms, physical functioning, participation, and health-related QoL, assessed using patient-reported outcome measures and physical performance tests. Complications were assessed using the Clavien-Dindo classification. Outcomes were assessed preoperatively as well as at 2 weeks, 6 weeks, 3 months, and 1 year postoperatively.
RESULTS: At 3 months, the proportion of patients achieving the PASS did not differ between the DAA and PLA for any HOOS subscales, including symptoms (65% [41 of 63] versus 63% [39 of 62], OR 1.03 [95% confidence interval (CI) 0.80 to 1.35]; p = 0.80), pain (48% [30 of 63] versus 53% [33 of 62], OR 0.90 [95% CI 0.63 to 1.27]; p = 0.53), activities of daily living (68% [43 of 63] versus 65% [40 of 62], OR 1.06 [95% CI 0.82 to 1.36]; p = 0.66), sports and recreation (55% [34 of 62] versus 58% [36 of 62], OR 0.94 [95% CI 0.69 to 1.29]; p = 0.72), and QoL (73% [46 of 63] versus 71% [44 of 62], OR 1.03 [95% CI 0.83 to 1.28]; p = 0.80). There were no between-group differences in symptoms, physical function, life activities and participation, and health-related QoL at any time point. Complications occurred in 8% (5 of 65) of patients in the DAA group and 2% (1 of 63) of patients in the PLA group (OR 3.05 [95% CI 0.51 to 18.40]; p = 0.21).
CONCLUSION: In this randomized controlled trial, the DAA did not improve patient-reported or functional outcomes compared with the PLA during the first postoperative year. In the absence of demonstrated patient-reported or functional benefits of the DAA, surgeons should not represent to patients that the DAA provides advantages in terms of the pace or magnitude of recovery. Future studies powered to detect differences in the risk of complications should be performed to see whether harms are more likely with the DAA than with other surgical approaches.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level I, therapeutic study.

title: Efficacy of combined therapies on degenerative joint disease of the temporomandibular joint: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the efficacy of intra-articular orthobiologics versus standard active control (arthrocentesis or hyaluronic acid) on pain, mouth opening and structural bone gain in advanced degenerative temporomandibular joint (TMJ) disease, stratified by orthobiologic class and joint compartment.
DESIGN: Systematic review with exploratory meta-analysis, following PRISMA and prospectively registered on PROSPERO (CRD420261425634), of RCTs published January 2020-June 2026. Outcomes were pooled as mean difference (MD) by orthobiologic class, with joint compartment as a three-level moderator. Clinical relevance was assessed against minimal important difference (MCID) thresholds; non-randomised studies were synthesised narratively.
RESULTS: Twenty-eight studies were included: 18 RCTs (≈862 patients; 12 pooled) and 10 narrative studies. Versus hyaluronic acid, orthobiologics reduced pain (MD -0.71) and improved mouth opening (MD 3.04 mm), both below the MCID. Versus arthrocentesis alone, effects were larger: pain (MD -1.57, exceeding the MCID) and mouth opening (MD 3.46 mm, below the MCID), with high heterogeneity unexplained by orthobiologic class. No RCT tested the dual joint space approach, represented only by one narrative study. A subset of studies had incomplete degenerative anchoring or unreported compartment. Certainty of evidence was low to very low.
CONCLUSIONS: Current evidence does not support a firm recommendation for any single orthobiologic in advanced degenerative TMJ disease, reinforcing a conservative, stepwise approach. Dual joint space therapy - a plausible but untested hypothesis - remains unstudied and is a priority for future research.

title: Is the number of strength and hop tests passed at the time of return to pre-injury sport level associated with second ACL injury? A registry study of 458 patients.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To analyze whether the number of strength and hop tests passed in a 5-test battery was associated with the hazard of second ACL injury after returning to pre-injury level of sports (RTS).
DESIGN: Registry-based cohort study.
SETTING: Data extracted in February 2026 from a rehabilitation registry.
PARTICIPANTS: Patients aged 15-35 years at the time of primary ACL reconstruction with ipsilateral hamstring or patellar tendon autograft and pre-injury Tegner activity level ≥ 6.
MAIN OUTCOME MEASURE: Second ACL injury after RTS, assessed during available follow-up and within one year of RTS using a Cox proportional hazard regression model. Hazard ratios with 95% confidence intervals were calculated and p-value was set to < 0.05.
RESULTS: 458 patients were included. 60 (13%) second ACL injuries occurred within all available follow-up time, where 32 (7.0%) occurred within 1 year after RTS. No significant association was observed between number of tests passed and second ACL injury during available follow-up (p = 0.41), or within one year of RTS (p = 0.87), after adjustment for autograft type, time to RTS, and BMI.
CONCLUSION: The number of tests passed in a 5-test muscle function battery was not associated with the hazard of second ACL injury after RTS.

title: Association between sleep difficulty and baseline concussion-like symptom burden in NCAA Division I athletes.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To examine the association between sleep difficulty and baseline concussion-like symptom burden among NCAA Division I athletes and whether sleep difficulty is associated with neurocognitive performance.
METHODS: This cross-sectional analysis included 584 NCAA Division I student-athletes. Sleep difficulty was assessed using the Athlete Sleep Screening Questionnaire Sleep Difficulty Score (SDS), and symptom burden using the 24-item SCOAT6 Symptom Evaluation. Symptom number was analyzed with multivariable negative binomial regression and symptom severity with multivariable linear regression using HC3 robust standard errors. Models adjusted for age, sex, sport type, and head-injury history. Sensitivity analyses excluded overlapping sleep-related symptoms and examined individual symptoms, symptom domains, head-injury strata, and neurocognitive outcomes.
RESULTS: Each 1-point increase in SDS was associated with greater symptom number (n = 583; IRR = 1.127, 95% CI 1.086-1.169, P < .001) and severity (n = 584; B = 1.054, 95% CI 0.688-1.419, P < .001). Associations persisted after excluding sleep disturbance and after additionally excluding fatigue/low energy and drowsiness. Twenty-one of 24 symptoms remained associated with SDS after false-discovery-rate correction. Head-injury history did not modify associations with symptom number (P = .971) or severity (P = .846). SDS was not associated with memory (B = -0.012, P = .269), executive function (B = -0.017, P = .247), or psychomotor speed (B = 0.001, P = .939).
CONCLUSIONS: Greater self-reported sleep difficulty was associated with greater baseline concussion-like symptom burden but not with assessed neurocognitive outcomes. Sleep difficulty should be considered a contextual factor when interpreting baseline concussion symptom reports.

title: Effects of repeated isometric exercise on pain-related and physical recovery outcomes following exercise-induced delayed onset muscle soreness in university athletes: A randomized sham-controlled trial.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate repeated quadriceps isometric exercise for recovery following experimentally induced delayed onset muscle soreness in university athletes.
DESIGN: Parallel-group, randomized sham-controlled trial.
METHODS: Forty university athletes were randomized to isometric exercise (n = 20) or sham exercise (n = 20). Co-primary outcomes were pressure pain threshold and soreness intensity; secondary outcomes were knee flexion range of motion, quadriceps isometric strength, and thigh circumference. Assessments occurred before and immediately after soreness induction and on Days 1, 3, and 5. Data were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models.
RESULTS: Significant Group × Time interactions were observed for soreness (P < 0.001, η2p = 0.898), pressure pain threshold (P < 0.001, η2p = 0.745), and knee flexion range of motion (P < 0.001, η2p = 0.378). Soreness was lower in the isometric group on Day 1 (mean difference, -2.55 points; 95% confidence interval -3.00 to -2.10; Hedges' g = -3.19) and Day 3 (-1.90 points; 95% confidence interval -2.35 to -1.45; Hedges' g = -2.74). Pressure pain threshold and knee flexion range of motion showed no significant between-group differences at individual time points. Group × Time interactions were not significant for quadriceps strength or thigh circumference.
CONCLUSIONS: Repeated submaximal isometric exercise was associated with lower perceived soreness during peak symptoms. Although pressure pain threshold and knee flexion range of motion showed different temporal patterns, neither differed significantly between groups at individual time points. Benefits for physical recovery outcomes remain uncertain.

title: Low Physical Therapy Referral Rates for Knee Osteoarthritis Present a Barrier to Care for Patients With Medicaid.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the rates of physical therapy (PT) referral for knee osteoarthritis (KOA) and factors associated with referral patterns, including insurance status, provider specialty, year, and patient demographics and comorbidities.
DESIGN: This retrospective cohort study included 41,373 patients diagnosed with KOA at an integrated health system in Arizona and Colorado, USA between January 2020 and February 2023. PT referral rates were stratified by insurance type. Multivariable logistic regression assessed predictors of referral including insurance type, age, BMI, sex, race/ethnicity, provider specialty, year of visit, and comorbidities.
RESULTS: Crude PT referral rates at the initial visit were 12.06% for Medicaid, 6.83% for Medicare, 10.29% for commercial insurance, and 8.33% for uninsured patients. Adjusted analysis showed that Medicaid patients had higher referral odds (OR, 1.20; 95% CI [1.10, 1.30]; p < 0.001), whereas Medicare patients had lower odds (OR, 0.76; 95% CI [0.66, 0.88]; p < 0.001) compared to those with commercial insurance. Female (OR, 1.21; 95% CI [1.14, 1.29]; p < 0.001) and Hispanic patients (OR 1.18; 95% CI [1.09, 1.29]; p < 0.001) demonstrated increased referral odds. Provider specialty was associated with PT referral, with non-operative sports medicine providers having the highest referral odds (OR, 3.00; 95% CI [2.72, 3.31]; p < 0.001) relative to orthopaedic surgery.
CONCLUSION: Despite strong clinical practice guidelines recommending PT, formal referral rates for patients with KOA remain low regardless of insurance type, patient characteristics, and referring healthcare provider specialty. Low formal PT referral rates may represent a barrier to evidence-based KOA care.

title: Traumatic brain injury, symptoms of depression and sleep dysfunction in former elite rugby players.
abstract: While self-reported repetitive head impact (RHI) exposure in former athletes has been associated with symptoms of depression and sleep dysfunction, it is uncertain whether these symptoms are mediated by changes in brain structure. We used cross-sectional data from 57 middle-aged, cognitively healthy, former elite rugby players and 114 propensity-matched controls. Questionnaires were used to collect self-reported traumatic brain injury (srTBI: blows to the head; episodes of feeling dazed and confused; episodes of loss of consciousness), RHI exposure (career length, play at the highest level and playing position), medical history, symptoms of depression (Center for Epidemiological Studies Depression scale) and sleep dysfunction (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index). Grey matter volumes and diffusion tensor imaging measures were obtained using FreeSurfer (v7.1.0, v7.4.2) and FSL (v6.0.5). We assessed how srTBI, RHI exposure, symptoms of depression, sleep dysfunction and the imaging markers were related using Spearman correlations, multivariate regression models and partial least squares structural equation modelling. Although former rugby players reported a higher number of blows to the head (9.8 versus 5.4, P < 0.001), number of episodes of feeling dazed and confused (4.5 versus 1.7, P < 0.001) and number of episodes of loss of consciousness (1.9 versus 0.7, P < 0.001), they were less likely to report a past diagnosis of anxiety (7% versus 22%, P = 0.03) or sleep disorders (2% versus 15%, P = 0.02) than controls. In rugby players, srTBI correlated poorly with RHI exposure. Furthermore, srTBI, but not RHI exposure, was associated with previous depression, anxiety and sleep disorders. Higher srTBI was directly associated with more symptoms of depression [B: 0.52 (95%CI: 0.21-0.74)], and indirectly associated with more sleep dysfunction [B: 0.18 (95%CI: 0.03-0.39)], fully mediated through symptoms of depression. Higher srTBI was also associated with a larger putamen (r = 0.28, P = 0.03) and inferior-tubular hypothalamus (r = 0.35, P = 0.007), thicker medial orbitofrontal (r = 0.32, P = 0.02) and insular cortices (r = 0.40, P = 0.002), lower axial diffusivity of the inferior cerebellar peduncle (r = -0.28, P = 0.03) and uncinate fasciculus (r = -0.26, P = 0.048), lower fractional anisotropy (r = -0.44, P < 0.001) and higher radial diffusivity (r = 0.29, P = 0.03) of the tapetum. Symptoms of depression were associated with thicker superior (r = 0.30, P = 0.02) and inferior (r = 0.33, P = 0.01) parietal cortices, higher fractional anisotropy of the hippocampal cingulum (r = 0.27, P = 0.04) and lower mean diffusivity of the fornix (r = -0.28, P = 0.03). None of these imaging markers mediated the association between srTBI and symptoms of depression. SrTBI, but not RHI exposure, was associated with symptoms of depression in former rugby players. However, this relationship was not mediated through differences in brain structure, suggesting that psychosocial or methodological factors such as recall bias and common method bias may be more important.

title: Sleep Characteristics of Elite Female Soccer Players Competing in the National Women's Soccer League Across a Competitive Season.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Sleep supports recovery and readiness in professional sport, yet season-long objective data in women's professional soccer are limited. This study aimed to provide a longitudinal, objective description of sleep across a competitive season and to compare sleep characteristics between preseason and in-season phases.
METHODS: Twenty-seven professional athletes were monitored from January to November 2024 using a finger-worn wearable. Nightly total sleep time (TST), sleep efficiency, sleep onset latency (SOL), and sleep stage durations were extracted. Preseason versus in-season differences were examined using linear mixed-effects models and reported as estimated marginal mean differences with 95% CIs.
RESULTS: During the in-season, TST averaged 7.8 (1.2) hours (median: 7.9 h), sleep efficiency 89.1% (5.4%), and SOL 15.6 (12.6) minutes. Mean sleep stage durations were 262.8 (52.8) minutes (light), 96.6 (31.8) minutes (deep), and 106.8 (34.2) minutes (Rapid Eye Movement). Notable night-to-night variability was observed, particularly for TST (within-player coefficients of variation: 10%-18%) and SOL (50%-114%). Compared with preseason, in-season sleep was characterized by lower REM sleep (-4.8 min, 95% CI -6.9 to -2.8; P < .001), reduced sleep efficiency (-0.37%, 95% CI -0.71 to -0.02; P = .036), and shorter SOL (-1.1 min, 95% CI -2.0 to -0.2; P = .020). TST did not differ between phases (P = .287), and deep and light sleep remained unchanged. Effect sizes were small (Cohen d ≤ 0.15).
CONCLUSIONS: Group averages of sleep parameters might mask individual and seasonal changes in sleep, highlighting the need for longitudinal, athlete-specific monitoring to guide proactive sleep monitoring strategies.

title: Interval Between Injury and Surgery Influences Knee Biomechanics During Walking in Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstructed Patients: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) is commonly performed to restore anatomical and functional knee stability. Although altered walking biomechanics have been observed post-ACLR, previous studies have not consistently accounted for the interval between injury and surgery.
OBJECTIVE: This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to determine whether walking-related knee biomechanical alterations following ACLR are transient or persist over time, and whether the timing of surgery influences these alterations.
METHODS: Five electronic databases (Scopus, PubMed, Web of Science, Physiotherapy Evidence Database [PEDro], and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials [CENTRAL]) were systematically searched from inception through August 2026. Studies comparing walking biomechanics between patients who underwent ACLR and healthy controls and reporting the interval between anterior cruciate ligament injury and reconstructive surgery were included. Biomechanical outcomes during the stance phase of walking were extracted and stratified according to the interval between injury and surgery: short term (0 to < 6 months), mid-term (6 to < 12 months), and long term (≥ 12 months). Standardized mean differences (SMDs) with 95% confidence intervals were calculated using a random-effects model. Study quality was assessed using a modified Downs and Black checklist.
RESULTS: Of the 3522 identified records, 16 studies involving male and female participants aged 18-55 years met the inclusion criteria. The mean methodological quality score was 65%, indicating an overall moderate level of methodological quality. Compared with healthy controls, ACLR participants demonstrated lower peak knee flexion angle (SMD = - 0.33, 95% confidence interval [CI] - 0.64 to - 0.02, p = 0.03, I2 = 57%), peak knee adduction angle (SMD = - 0.47, 95% CI - 0.92 to - 0.01, p = 0.04, I2 = 66%), and peak knee flexion moment (SMD = - 0.64, 95% CI - 1.05 to - 0.23, p = 0.002, I2 = 76%). In subgroup analyses, the long-term group (≥ 12 months between injury and surgery) demonstrated lower peak knee flexion angle (SMD = - 0.27, 95% CI - 0.54 to - 0.00, p = 0.05, I2 = 8%) and peak knee flexion moment (SMD = - 1.97, 95% CI - 3.77 to - 0.17, p = 0.03, I2 = 88%). The short-term group (0 to < 6 months) demonstrated lower peak knee adduction angle (SMD = - 0.79, 95% CI - 1.18 to - 0.40, p < 0.0001, I2 = 19%) and peak knee extension moment (SMD = - 0.55, 95% CI - 0.93 to - 0.18, p = 0.004, I2 = 50%).
CONCLUSIONS: The interval between anterior cruciate ligament injury and ACLR was associated with differences in postoperative walking biomechanics. Delayed reconstruction (≥ 12 months) is associated with persistent sagittal plane deficits, which may reflect chronic neuromuscular adaptations or preoperative joint degeneration. In contrast, early surgery (within 6 months after anterior cruciate ligament injury) was associated with fewer long-term sagittal-plane deficits, although temporary frontal-plane asymmetries and extension deficits may persist during the early postoperative period and may improve with rehabilitation. These findings underscore the importance of considering the timing of ACLR when planning surgery and postoperative rehabilitation to support walking recovery.

title: Temporal dynamics of the repeated bout effect on exercise-induced muscle damage: a systematic review and three-level meta-analysis.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: The repeated bout effect (RBE) confers protection against exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD). However, the temporal profile of this protective response both across post-exercise recovery and across different intervention-to-damage intervals remains poorly defined. This three-level meta-analysis aimed to quantify the time-course of RBE protective effects and to characterize potential temporal windows for intervention and measurement.
METHODS: A systematic search of PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and Scopus (inception to June 2025) identified 35 eligible studies. Three outcome measures, maximal voluntary contraction (MVC), delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS), and creatine kinase (CK), were analyzed using three-level random-effects models. Effect sizes (Hedges' g) were stratified by post-exercise measurement time (24, 48, 72, and 96 h) and intervention interval (<1 week, 1-2 weeks, 2-3 weeks, and >3 weeks).
RESULTS: RBE significantly protected MVC (overall g = 1.18, 95% CI: 0.91-1.45) and reduced DOMS (g = -1.37, 95% CI: -1.70 to -1.05) and CK (g = -0.91, 95% CI: -1.33 to -0.50). Time-stratified analyses revealed distinct temporal patterns. MVC and DOMS showed their largest observed protective estimates at 72 h post-damage (g = 1.47 and -1.65, respectively), whereas CK showed its largest observed protective estimate at 96 h (g = -1.53). Direct comparisons accounting for within-study dependence showed a larger MVC estimate at 72 h than at 48 h and a more protective CK estimate at 48 h than at 24 h. Subgroup analyses revealed outcome-specific interval patterns, with pooled protective effects for MVC and DOMS numerically smallest in magnitude in the 2-3-week subgroup at all four assessed time points.
CONCLUSION: RBE-related protection showed time-dependent patterns across outcomes. Among the assessed time points, pooled protective effects were largest in magnitude at 72 h for functional (MVC) and perceptual (DOMS) outcomes, whereas biochemical (CK) effects increased progressively in magnitude through 96 h. The 2-3-week interval was characterized by numerically weaker pooled protective effects for MVC and DOMS. These findings provide an evidence-informed temporal framework for optimizing preconditioning and recovery-monitoring strategies in athletic training.

title: Risk, Knowledge, and Awareness of Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (RED-S) in Elite Female Volleyball Players.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S) is a condition caused by low energy availability (LEA) and is associated with adverse health and performance outcomes in athletes. Although volleyball involves considerable physical stress and repetitive jumping, little is known about RED-S knowledge and risk of LEA in elite female volleyball players.
HYPOTHESIS: Elite female volleyball athletes have limited awareness of RED-S, and athletes at risk for LEA according to the LEAF-Q are more likely to be injured.
STUDY DESIGN: Cross-sectional study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 3.
METHODS: Elite female volleyball athletes competing in the Turkish Women's Elite Volleyball League during the 2024-2025 season were recruited. Participants completed an online survey including demographic information, the Low Energy Availability in Females Questionnaire (LEAF-Q), and items assessing knowledge, awareness, and support-seeking behaviors related to RED-S. Athletes were classified as "at risk" for LEA using a LEAF-Q cutoff score of ≥8. Associations between LEAF-Q risk status and injury history during the previous year were analyzed.
RESULTS: A total of 148 athletes participated. The mean LEAF-Q score was 5.50 ± 3.48, and 25% of athletes were classified as at risk for LEA according to the LEAF-Q. Most athletes (92.6%) reported never having heard of RED-S or the Female Athlete Triad. Athletes identified as at risk by the LEAF-Q were significantly more likely to have sustained an injury in the previous year than athletes not at risk (odds ratio, 7.86; 95% CI, 3.03-20.41).
CONCLUSION: Elite female volleyball athletes demonstrated low knowledge of RED-S, while a substantial proportion were identified as at risk for LEA. LEA risk was associated strongly with injury history, supporting the clinical relevance of LEAF-Q screening in this population.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Routine LEAF-Q screening combined with sport-specific education may facilitate early identification of athletes who may require further clinical evaluation for LEA-related problems and may inform prevention-oriented support strategies in elite female volleyball players.

title: Prevalence and predictors of in-class dozing among collegiate athletes and non-athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Adequate sleep is critical for recovery and performance, yet athletes often experience less sleep than non-athletes, potentially impacting their academic performance. This study investigates the prevalence and factors in-class dozing among collegiate athletes compared to non-athletes.
METHODS: This cross-sectional study surveyed 165 athletes and 92 non-athletes using an anonymous online questionnaire, focusing on sleep duration, commute times, part-time employment, and attitudes towards sleeping in class.
RESULTS: Athletes reported a higher frequency of in-class dozing (70.4%) compared to non-athletes (55.5%, P=0.009). The primary reason for in-class dozing among athletes was fatigue from sports practice, whereas non-athletes attributed it to part-time work. Logistic regression analysis revealed that athletes had a higher risk of in-class dozing (OR=2.71, 95% CI 1.42-5.16, P=0.002), and both younger age (OR=0.46, 95% CI 0.24-0.87, P=0.016) and insufficient sleep at night (OR=0.71, 95% CI 0.55-0.92, P=0.010) were associated with increased risk.
CONCLUSIONS: Both athletes and non-athletes are not obtaining adequate sleep, with athletes particularly affected by training-related fatigue possibly causing in-class dozing. Factors contributing to the likelihood of in-class dozing included younger age, inadequate nightly sleep, being an athlete, and engagement in part-time employment.

title: Severe injuries in competitive cycling during an olympic cycle: injury patterns, time loss, and return-to-performance outcomes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cycling is an established Olympic sport associated with a distinct injury profile that has not yet been comprehensively investigated. This study aimed to retrospectively assess and analyze severe cycling-related injuries resulting in ≥ 3 weeks of time loss over a complete Olympic cycle.
METHODS: A total of 192 cyclists were included, based on a retrospective online questionnaire assessing injury location, type, context, time loss, and return-to-sport outcomes. Comparisons by sex, discipline, and competitive level were performed at the athlete level using exact tests with 95% confidence intervals and were considered exploratory.
RESULTS: Seventy-two of 192 athletes sustained at least one severe injury over the five-year period, corresponding to a proportion of 37.5% (95% CI 31.0-44.5). A total of 237 injuries were recorded, with the upper extremity (33.8%) and lower extremity (27.8%) being the most frequently affected regions. The most common diagnoses were hand fractures (n = 14), clavicle fractures (n = 13), and non-specific knee injuries (n = 9). Hand fractures (33.3%; p = 0.002) and shoulder dislocations (20.0%; p = 0.002) were most frequent among BMX athletes, while hand fractures also occurred more frequently in competitive athletes than in recreational athletes (13.5% vs. 1.0%; p = 0.001). Clavicle fractures occurred predominantly during competition and non-specific knee injuries during training. Mean time loss ranged from 6.5 weeks for hand fractures to 13.3 weeks for shoulder dislocations. Full return to pre-injury performance ranged from 85.7% after hand fractures to 28.6% after acromioclavicular (AC) joint separations.
CONCLUSION: Injury patterns differed by discipline and setting, suggesting that prevention strategies should address both. The low rate of full return to performance after AC joint separations despite moderate time loss underlines the importance of distinguishing return to sport from return to performance in rehabilitation.

title: The Impact of Tourniquet Duration on Postoperative Opioid Use and Recovery After Total Knee Arthroplasty.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Tourniquet use during total knee arthroplasty (TKA) remains common, but its effects on postoperative pain, opioid use, and stiffness are unclear. We evaluated whether tourniquet duration was associated with pain- and stiffness-related outcomes after primary TKA.
METHODS: We performed a retrospective study of 17,850 adults undergoing primary unilateral TKA at a single center from March 2016 to June 2023. Tourniquet use was categorized by inflation time relative to operative time as no tourniquet (n = 1,243), partial tourniquet (less than 0.6; n = 2,914), tourniquet-until-arthrotomy-closure (≥ 0.6 to less than 1; n = 10,003), or full-duration tourniquet (≥ 1; n = 3,690). The primary outcome was postoperative pain assessed by postoperative inpatient and cumulative 90-day morphine milligram equivalents (MME). The secondary outcomes were hours to clear physical therapy (PT), manipulation under anesthesia (MUA) within 120 days, and patient-reported Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score for Joint Replacement (KOOS JR) at six weeks. Multivariable regressions adjusted for covariates. The no-tourniquet group served as the reference.
RESULTS: Partial-tourniquet use was associated with lower 90-day opioid consumption (-90 MME; 95% confidence interval (CI) -150 to -30; P = 0.003). Tourniquet-until-closure and full-duration tourniquet were associated with higher inpatient opioid consumption (+10 MMEs; 95% CI, 2 to 17; P = 0.015; and +14 MMEs; 95% CI, 6 to 22; P = 0.001), longer time to PT clearance (+2.7 hours, 95% CI, 1.0 to 4.5; P = 0.002; and +4.1 hours, 95% CI, 2.2 to 5.9; P < 0.001), and higher adjusted odds (OR) of MUA (OR 1.78, 95% CI, 1.14 to 2.79; P = 0.012; and OR 1.64, 95% CI, 1.02 to 2.64; P = 0.040). Partial-tourniquet use was not associated with increased time to clear PT or increased odds of MUA. The KOOS JR scores did not differ significantly across strategies.
CONCLUSIONS: Tourniquet use during TKA showed duration-dependent associations with postoperative outcomes. Partial-tourniquet use may represent a balanced strategy, associated with lower cumulative 90-day opioid consumption without the delayed PT clearance or increased MUA risk observed with longer-duration tourniquet strategies.

title: Eating Behavior, Body Appreciation, and Sleep Quality in Italian Blind Baseball Athletes: A Cross-Sectional Exploratory Survey.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Visual impairment is associated with poor sleep quality, psychological distress, and unhealthy lifestyle behaviors. Adapted sports, such as blind baseball (BXC), may help promote healthy lifestyles and overall well-being. However, evidence regarding eating behavior, sleep quality, body appreciation, and lifestyle habits among regular BXC players remains scarce. This cross-sectional study provides an exploratory multidimensional characterization of these domains in competitive Italian BXC athletes according to sport participation and visual impairment characteristics, comparing findings descriptively with normative data from the Italian general population. Methods: Fifty-three competitive Italian BXC players (mean age 39.3 ± 13.1 years; representing a response rate of 49.1% of the national league) completed an anonymous online survey assessing eating behavior (Adult Eating Behavior Questionnaire, AEBQ), body appreciation (Body Appreciation Scale-2, BAS-2), sleep quality (Brief Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, B-PSQI), and lifestyle habits. Group differences were assessed using chi-square tests for categorical variables and Mann-Whitney U tests for continuous variables, reporting medians, interquartile ranges, effect sizes (rank-biserial r), and 95% confidence intervals. Results: BXC athletes demonstrated BMI, sleep quality, eating behavior, and body appreciation profiles comparable to those of the Italian general population. BAS-2 scores were high (3.7-3.8), while B-PSQI scores (4.0-5.6) and the proportion of poor sleepers (~40%) remained within normative ranges despite visual impairment. Eating behavior showed no significant dysregulation. However, in exploratory subgroup analyses, multisport athletes displayed lower Satiety Responsiveness than BXC-only athletes (2.30 ± 0.79 vs. 2.78 ± 0.71; p = 0.02), poorer sleep quality (B-PSQI: 6.05 ± 3.12 vs. 4.70 ± 3.73; p = 0.05), and a higher prevalence of poor sleep (55.0% vs. 30.3%). Athletes with acquired visual impairment showed higher Emotional Overeating and Emotional Undereating scores than those with congenital impairment, although these differences did not reach statistical significance. Conclusions: BXC athletes displayed an overall favorable lifestyle profile. Though the cross-sectional design prevents causal inferences, these exploratory findings indicate that participation in BXC is compatible with healthy lifestyle habits and positive body appreciation, hence supporting adapted team sports as an inclusive framework for multidimensional health promotion. Future studies using objective physiological assessments and longitudinal designs are needed to clarify dose-response relationships and long-term health outcomes.

title: Global Positioning System-Derived Match Demands and Their Association With On-Field Technical Performance in Elite Australian Football League Women's (AFLW) Athletes.
abstract:
PURPOSE: This study sought to determine the associations between global positioning system-derived match demands and technical performance in elite Australian Football League Women's athletes.
METHODS: Global positioning system match demands (total distance, speed, acceleration, high-intensity running [>19 km·h-1], very high-intensity running [>21 km·h-1], sprint distances [>24 km·h-1]) were measured with Catapult Vector S7 global positioning system units during the 2023 and 2024 seasons. Champion Data ranking points and best and fairest votes for each game were considered technical performance outcomes. Linear mixed effects regression models examined associations between match demands and technical performance, adjusting for season, ground location, and playing position.
RESULTS: Five hundred sixty-six player match profiles from 32 athletes across the 2 seasons were analyzed. Ranking points were significantly (P < .001) associated with total distance (R2 = .29 [95% CI .22-.40]), speed (R2 = .01 [.00-.15]), and acceleration (R2 = .09 [.00-.23]). Best and fairest votes were significantly (P < .001) associated with total distance (R2 = .23 [.17-.34]), speed (R2 = .01 [.00-.11]), acceleration (R2 = .05 [.00-.17]), and very high-intensity running distance per minute (R2 = .00 [.00-.13]).
CONCLUSIONS: Total distance, speed, acceleration, and very high-intensity running distance per minute were associated with Champion Data ranking points and best and fairest votes across Australian Football League Women's seasons 2023 and 2024. This suggests that athletes who cover greater total distances and achieve higher average acceleration get more opportunities to be involved in match-play and demonstrate higher levels of technical performance.

title: Adaptive training load optimization for sprinters via offline reinforcement learning and multi-modal physiological feedback.
abstract: Elite sprint training requires daily adjustment of training load to balance performance adaptation and fatigue, yet physiological monitoring does not necessarily translate into a specific next-session prescription. This study formalizes daily sprint training prescription as a finite-horizon Markov Decision Process and develops an adaptive load-optimization framework that couples multi-modal physiological feedback with offline reinforcement learning (RL). A 19-dimensional state fusing autonomic, neuromuscular, endocrine, subjective, and load-aggregate signals is encoded by a dual-tower network [a one-dimensional convolutional neural network-Transformer temporal branch and a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) static branch] over an action space of 62 admissible training-type/intensity/volume combinations. A composite reward penalizes overreaching while rewarding short-term gain, longitudinal adaptation, and acute-to-chronic workload ratio conformity. The policy is learned by conservative off-policy training on retrospective data, evaluated through the Fitted Q-Evaluation (FQE) and Doubly Robust (DR) estimators, and presented to coaches as the three leading candidate actions, with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) values used to explain the model's preferences among the candidate actions. In a 12-week single-center retrospective comparison of 70 national-level sprinters (35 men and 35 women; 100 m personal best (PB) ≤ 11.20 s for men or ≤ 12.50 s for women), grouped by whether their squad had adopted the tool (n = 35 RL-guided) or continued classical block periodisation (n = 35 control), the RL-guided cohort demonstrated between-cohort differences of +0.240 s in 100 m [95% confidence interval (CI) +0.128 to +0.352; p < 0.001, d = 1.00], +0.104 s in 30 m (p < 0.001, d = 1.00) and +2.17 cm in countermovement jump (p < 0.001, d = 1.01). Zero algorithmically defined sustained multi-indicator fatigue/load events were observed in the RL-guided cohort vs. seven in the control cohort (1.43 per 1,000 athlete-days); these events should not be interpreted as clinically diagnosed overtraining syndrome. Off-policy evaluation yielded exploratory point estimates whose precision remains unknown because uncertainty intervals were not calculated. These observational findings describe associations with an RL-guided, coach-in-the-loop workflow and do not establish a causal effect of the RL policy.

title: Collective case study on periodized training in elite female middle- and long-distance swimmers preparing for national competition.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Elite swimmers increasingly face calendars requiring multiple performance peaks within a single season, a scenario for which traditional single-target periodization models may be insufficient.
METHODS: This longitudinal collective case study followed five elite female middle- and long-distance freestyle swimmers across a 52-week macrocycle preparing for two national championships. The program combined three altitude camps, sea-level integration phases and two timed tapers. Training intensity distribution (TID) was quantified with a three-zone lactate-threshold model; hemoglobin, hematocrit, red blood cell count, creatine kinase and cortisol were measured at four time points; and performance was assessed by time-trial and official competition results. Given N = 5, analysis prioritized a smallest-worthwhile-change (SWC) classification for performance and paired effect sizes with 95% confidence intervals for blood markers rather than null-hypothesis significance testing. Hematological outcomes are concentration-based indices; training-load descriptors refer to in-water swimming only.
RESULTS: Applying an SWC of ≈0.24% to the 20 athlete-by-event observations, 12/20 (60%) changes at Competition 1 and 18/20 (90%) at Competition 2 exceeded the SWC, most representing improvement over baseline; this ordering held across the full defensible range of reference variability (SWC 0.22-0.42%). Hematological effect sizes were largest at Week 27 (RBC: Hedges' g = 2.32, 95% CI [0.64, 4.01]; HCT: g = 2.04 [0.50, 3.58]), while creatine kinase and cortisol peaked at Week 17 and were closer to baseline at Week 49, compatible with a lower physiological stress state at that sampled time point. TID shifted across phases (pyramidal during base development, polarized during altitude blocks, threshold-oriented during race-pace sharpening), with marked inter-individual heterogeneity in performance and physiological responses.
CONCLUSION: Across this double-peak macrocycle, most athlete-by-event changes exceeded the SWC, and the proportion doing so was higher at the second championship than at the first; these changes occurred alongside altitude-associated increases in concentration-based oxygen-transport indices and a taper-associated normalization of creatine kinase and cortisol. With no control group or randomization, only five athletes and four blood samples, several simultaneous interventions and unmeasured confounders (iron status, menstrual-cycle phase, dryland load), these findings describe associations only. They are offered as exploratory, hypothesis-generating observations from a single elite squad rather than as causal evidence.

title: Baseline Symptom Collection in Elite Rugby Union Players-Limited Clinical Utility? An Investigation of Assessments Across 5879 men and Women Athletes.
abstract: In World Rugby's Head Injury Assessment (HIA) protocol, a modified Sports Concussion Assessment Tool (SCAT) is completed during the pre-season (baseline) and when a player has a suspected head injury. The symptom component of the SCAT, which involves comparing current to baseline symptoms, has been shown to be the most predictive component for concussion diagnosis. Because the clinical comparison of symptom report to baseline is a key determinant of concussion diagnosis, this study aims to explore the relationship between symptoms endorsement at baseline and during HIA. Mean and standard deviation (SD) or median and interquartile ranges (IQR) are presented along with relevant bivariate analyses. Logistic regressions compared proportions of symptom endorsement profiles between men and women. At baseline, 'Trouble sleeping' and 'Fatigue or low energy' were commonly reported symptoms for men and women. At baseline, women (mean + SD) reported more symptoms than men (mean + SD) on average. During the HIA, women players were nearly 3 times (Relative risk: 2.98 95% CIs: 2.47-3.60) more likely than men to report fewer symptoms immediately after the match than at baseline (47% women vs. 16% men). While this study highlights the importance of collecting baseline assessment as a medical overview of players, it de-emphasises the relevance of baseline symptoms when using the SCAT as a clinical assessment tool in professional rugby players. This study also highlights important differences in men and women's rugby players in symptom reporting, and recommends de-coupling baseline symptom reporting from the diagnostic part of the HIA.

title: The role of scapular muscles strengthening in lateral epicondylalgia rehabilitation: A systematic review with meta-analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Lateral epicondylalgia is a prevalent tendinopathy often recurring despite conventional physiotherapy. Emerging evidence suggests that scapular muscles strengthening improves outcomes by addressing proximal kinetic chain deficits.
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the effectiveness of scapular muscles strengthening combined with conventional physiotherapy compared with conventional physiotherapy alone in patients with Lateral epicondylalgia.
STUDY DESIGN: Systematic review with meta-analysis.
METHODS: Following PRISMA guidelines, PubMed, PEDro, Scopus, Web of Science and ScienceDirect were searched up to January 2026. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and non-randomized experimental studies with Lateral Epicondylalgia were included. Outcomes were pain (Visual Analog Scale, Numeric Pain Rating Scale), grip strength (dynamometer), and function {pain and disability (Patient-Rated Tennis Elbow Evaluation)}. Methodological quality was assessed using Physiotherapy Evidence Database (PEDro) scale and Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) appraisal tool. Risk of bias was evaluated using Revised Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool for Randomized Trials and Risk of Bias in Non-Randomized Studies of interventions, and certainty of evidence using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach.
RESULTS: Twelve studies [10 RCTs, 2 non-randomized) were included, with 8 RCTs pooled for meta-analysis. Scapular muscles strengthening plus conventional therapy demonstrated significant functional improvement (PRTEE: MD = -9.33; 95% CI -15.01 to -3.65; p = 0.001; I² = 73%). No significant pooled effect was found for pain (SMD = -0.36; 95% CI -1.24-0.52; p = 0.43; I² = 86%) or grip strength (SMD = 0.19; 95% CI -0.09-0.47; p = 0.18). Overall low to moderate risk of bias, with good RCTs quality (PEDro mean score=6/10) and high non- RCTs quality (JBI). Overall certainty of evidence was moderate for pain and grip strength and low for PRTEE.
CONCLUSION: Scapular muscles strengthening combined with conventional physiotherapy provides superior functional outcomes compared with conventional therapy alone in patients with LE. Effects on pain and grip strength remain inconclusive.

title: Pre-sleep milk-derived proteins do not impair sleep or recovery in elite female athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sleep is essential for athlete recovery and performance, yet athletes frequently experience restricted or poor-quality sleep. Pre-sleep feeding (PSF) has emerged as a strategy to support recovery, but randomized, double-blinded, crossover trials comparing PSF macronutrient options on objective and subjective sleep outcomes in elite female athletes remain limited.
METHODS: Twenty-five National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) Division I female athletes (18-25 years old) were recruited; 21 completed the trial. In a randomized, double-blinded, placebo controlled, crossover design conducted over 4-8 weeks, participants consumed four treatments for three consecutive nights each: 40 g casein protein (CAS; 160 kcal), 40 g α-lactalbumin protein (ALA; 160 kcal), 40 g carbohydrate (CHO; 160 kcal), and 40g of a placebo (PLA; 5 kcal), with a minimum three-day washout between conditions. Supplements were consumed ~2 h after the final meal and ~30 min before bedtime as the last caloric intake of the day. Objective outcomes were obtained from the WHOOP 4.0 device (total sleep time (TST), sleep onset latency (SOL), sleep efficiency (SE), resting heart rate (RHR), and heart rate variability (HRV)). Subjective outcomes were assessed each morning via questionnaires (subjective sleep quality (SSQ), subjective sleep onset latency (SSOL), and subjective recovery (SREC)). Nocturnal interstitial glucose was assessed via blinded continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) in a subset (n = 6). Sleep and recovery variables were analyzed using one-way repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) to evaluate treatment effects across the four supplementation conditions. For CGM data, a two-way repeated-measures ANOVA was used to evaluate main effects of treatment and time, as well as the treatment × time interaction. Tukey's post hoc testing was used with significance set at p < 0.05.
RESULTS: No significant treatment effects were observed for TST, SOL, SE, RHR, or HRV (p > 0.05). TST ranged from 7.47-7.62 h, SE from 91.5-92.0%, RHR from 53.5-54.1 bpm, and HRV from 98.2-103.9 ms across conditions. No significant treatment effects were detected for SSQ, SSOL, or SREC (p > 0.05); SSQ ranged from 69-75%, SSOL from 16-20 min, and SREC from 61-66%. In the CGM sub-analysis, a main effect of time was observed for nocturnal glucose (p = 0.008), but no differences among treatments (p = 0.187) or a time × treatment interaction (p = 0.550) were detected.
CONCLUSIONS: In NCAA Division I female athletes, three consecutive nights of pre-sleep ingestion of CAS, ALA, or CHO did not impair objective or subjective measures of sleep or recovery compared with PLA. These findings demonstrate that pre-sleep feeding, regardless of macronutrient type, can be incorporated without negatively affecting sleep quality or recovery metrics.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov (Identifier: STUDY00004409).

title: Cold-Water Immersion for Post-exercise Recovery: An Overlap-Aware Umbrella Review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cold-water immersion (CWI) is widely used after strenuous exercise, but review-level findings vary by outcome, comparator, recovery window, population, and protocol. Reuse of the same primary studies across reviews can also exaggerate apparent consistency.
METHODS: We searched PubMed, Web of Science, SPORTDiscus, Cochrane Library, Embase, and Scopus from inception to 30 January 2026 for systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and network meta-analyses of post-exercise CWI. Fourteen reviews were included. Primary-study overlap was quantified using the corrected covered area (CCA) overall and for outcome-specific study-to-review mappings. Because overlap was high and review-level estimates were statistically dependent, we did not perform second-order meta-analysis. Source-verified estimates were synthesized in a structured, overlap-aware format. Methodological quality was assessed with AMSTAR 2.
RESULTS: Of the 14 included reviews, 13 provided quantitative estimates, whereas one review provided narrative evidence on heart rate variability (HRV). Overall CCA was 12.68% (high); 99 of 165 primary-study families appeared in at least two reviews. Outcome-specific CCA was 15.03% for delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS; very high) and ranged from 0.00% for interleukin-6 (IL-6) to 25.00% for C-reactive protein (CRP). It was not calculable for HRV, because one review contributed. AMSTAR 2 confidence was low in 2 reviews and critically low in 12. DOMS showed the most consistent favorable pattern: source-review standardized mean differences ranged from -1.04 to -0.37, although the largest estimate was soccer-specific and its 95% prediction interval crossed zero. Because DOMS evidence was highly redundant across the contributing reviews, this apparent consistency does not represent independent replications. Findings for objective performance and biochemical outcomes were inconsistent, time-dependent, or comparator-dependent.
CONCLUSIONS: Within the available review-level evidence, CWI was associated with the most consistent reduction in self-reported short-term post-exercise DOMS, but the clinical importance of the observed effects remains uncertain. Evidence does not support a uniform benefit across objective performance or inflammatory outcomes. Protocol observations, including commonly studied temperatures and durations, are descriptive and should not be interpreted as an optimized prescription. Trial Registration PROSPERO CRD420261332482.

title: Short-term Rhodiola rosea supplementation improves premenstrual symptoms, reaction time, and perceived exertion in female taekwondo athletes: a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Premenstrual symptoms may negatively influence psychological readiness, cognitive-motor performance, and perceived exertion in female athletes. Rhodiola rosea (RR) is an adaptogenic herb that has been investigated for its potential effects on fatigue, stress tolerance, mood, and exercise-related outcomes. However, its effects on premenstrual symptoms and performance-related responses in female athletes remain unclear. This study aimed to investigate the effects of short-term RR supplementation during the estimated symptomatic premenstrual phase on premenstrual symptoms, peripheral serum serotonin and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) concentrations, reaction time, perceived exertion, and aerobic performance-related indices in female taekwondo athletes with premenstrual syndrome (PMS).
METHODS: In this randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 24 female taekwondo athletes with moderate-to-severe PMS symptoms were randomly assigned to receive either 500 mg/day of standardised RR extract (n = 12) or placebo (n = 12) for 10 days during the estimated symptomatic premenstrual phase. Premenstrual symptoms were assessed using the Premenstrual Symptoms Screening Tool (PSST). Visual reaction time, peripheral serum serotonin and GABA concentrations, time to exhaustion (TTE), estimated VO₂max, and rating of perceived exertion (RPE) were evaluated before and after the intervention. Data were analysed using analysis of covariance with baseline values as covariates.
RESULTS: Compared with placebo, RR supplementation significantly reduced several PMS symptoms, including irritability, depression, anxiety, social withdrawal, decreased concentration, hypersomnia, food cravings, crying, skin problems, and abdominal pain (p < 0.05). The RR group demonstrated faster reaction time compared with placebo (adjusted mean difference: -60 ms; p < 0.001). Peripheral serum serotonin and GABA concentrations were significantly higher in the RR group than in the placebo group (p < 0.001). In addition, RR supplementation reduced post-exercise RPE (adjusted mean difference: -1.40 Borg units; p = 0.006). However, no significant differences were observed between groups in TTE or estimated VO₂max (p > 0.05).
CONCLUSION: Short-term RR supplementation during the estimated symptomatic premenstrual phase may improve selected PMS symptoms, visual reaction time, and perceived exertion in female taekwondo athletes with PMS. Larger trials with hormonal confirmation of menstrual cycle phase, longer intervention periods, direct physiological measurements, and sport-specific performance assessments are required to confirm these findings.

title: Effects of different recovery and regeneration modalities on delayed-onset muscle soreness and post-exercise muscle damage markers: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This study employed a systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis to compare the effects of multiple post-exercise interventions during the early recovery period, examine whether these effects varied across recovery time points, and provide evidence to inform the selection of post-exercise recovery strategies.
METHODS: PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and Web of Science were systematically searched, and randomized controlled trials, including parallel-group and crossover designs, were included. A Bayesian random-effects network meta-analysis was used to estimate mean differences (MDs) and 95% credible intervals (CrIs). The revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomized trials (RoB 2) and the Confidence in Network Meta-Analysis (CINeMA) framework were used to assess risk of bias and confidence in the evidence, respectively. Sensitivity analyses and exploratory univariable network meta-regression analyses were also performed.
RESULTS: A total of 35 studies were included in this review. For delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS), whole-body cryotherapy (WBC) and photobiomodulation/phototherapy-related interventions (PHO) showed relatively large reductions in soreness at both 24 and 48 h after exercise. Compared with the combined control/placebo condition (CON/PBO), the effect estimates for WBC were MD = -38.92 (95% CrI: -69.08 to -9.15) at 24 h and MD = -40.03 (95% CrI: -67.74 to -12.44) at 48 h. The corresponding estimates for PHO were MD = -18.20 (95% CrI: -32.91 to -3.72) and MD = -19.46 (95% CrI: -33.55 to -5.99), respectively. For creatine kinase (CK), low-level laser therapy (LLLT) and PHO were associated with lower CK levels at both 24 and 48 h, with the largest estimated effect for LLLT at 48 h (MD = -499.96, 95% CrI: -831.59 to -203.59). For interleukin-6 (IL-6), CWI showed favorable estimates at both 24 and 48 h, although the evidence base was limited and the network was sparse.
CONCLUSION: WBC and PHO showed relatively consistent favorable effects on DOMS at 24 and 48 h, whereas LLLT and PHO showed relatively consistent associations with lower CK levels. The IL-6 findings should be interpreted as exploratory because of the limited evidence base. Selection of post-exercise recovery strategies should consider the target outcome, recovery time window, evidence certainty, and network structure.

title: Exercise Endurance Effects of Food-Derived Polysaccharides in Animal Models of Exercise-Induced Fatigue: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: The effects of food-derived polysaccharides on endurance may depend on their source materials, extraction and purification procedures, molecular characteristics, and mode of administration; however, their average effects and transferability across animal models remain uncertain. To quantify effects on exercise endurance and to evaluate how chemical/process characterization, biochemical response domains, and evidence quality support functional-food interpretation. Controlled animal studies were systematically reviewed; 31 independent StudyIDs from 30 reports were synthesized using random-effects response ratios (RoM) with Hartung-Knapp intervals. Chemical and processing descriptors and selected biochemical outcomes were mapped as structured evidence layers. Endurance increased overall (RoM 1.707, 95% CI 1.540-1.892; I 2 = 95.4%), while the 95% prediction interval (0.999-2.917) included the null. Characterization was incomplete: purity/content, molecular weight, monosaccharide composition, and extraction or purification information were recoverable for only subsets of StudyIDs. Biochemical observations clustered around energy-substrate, lactate/BUN, oxidative-stress, muscle-injury, mitochondrial/AMPK, and gut-microbiota domains, but few comparable records were suitable for effect-size calculation. Food-derived polysaccharides show a positive average preclinical endurance signal, but very high heterogeneity, incomplete chemical/process reporting, evidence asymmetry, and sparse harmonized biochemical data constrain claims of efficacy for formulated functional foods.

title: Dose-response relationship between training volume and outcomes for hip osteoarthritis: Exploratory study from The Hip Booster Trial.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To explore associations between training volume and changes in patient-reported hip pain and physical function, performance-based function, and muscle power in patients with hip osteoarthritis.
DESIGN: Exploratory cohort study with data from The HipBooster Trial.
SETTING: Five hospitals and 10 physiotherapy clinics across Denmark.
PARTICIPANTS: 144 of 160 patients who had complete training and outcome data.
INTERVENTIONS: Participants were randomized to 12 weeks of twice-weekly progressive resistance training (PRT) or neuromuscular exercise (NEMEX).
MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: Hip disability and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (HOOS) pain and Activities of Daily Living (ADL), 30-s chair stand test (30s-CST), and leg extensor power (LEP) assessed at baseline and post-intervention.
RESULTS: In the PRT group, each 10 000 kg increase in total training volume across 24 sessions was associated with an increase of 1.13 (95% CI: -0.01; 2.26) points for HOOS pain, 1.33 (95% CI: 0.26; 2.39) for HOOS ADL, 0.12 (95% CI: -0.10; 0.33) repetitions in the 30s-CST, and 2.37 (95% CI: -0.68; 5.43) watts in LEP. In the NEMEX group, each 2000 repetitions increase in total training volume was associated with an increase of 1.12 (95% CI: -0.61; 2.85) points for HOOS pain, 1.92 (95% CI: 0.13; 3.70) for HOOS ADL, 0.31 (95% CI: -0.08; 0.70) repetitions in the 30s-CST, and -1.25 (95% CI: -5.92; 3.43) watts in LEP.
CONCLUSION: Greater total training volume seems associated with slightly greater improvements in pain and physical function in hip osteoarthritis. These findings should be interpreted cautiously, given the exploratory nature of the study.

title: Associations between demographic characteristics and Big Five personality traits after anterior cruciate ligament injury: A registry-based cross-sectional study.
abstract:
PURPOSE: The purpose of this study was to investigate associations between demographic characteristics and personality traits, measured with the Big Five Inventory-2 (BFI-2), in patients after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury. A secondary exploratory purpose was to compare demographic characteristics across groups defined by predominant personality trait.
METHODS: Data for this cross-sectional study were obtained from a Swedish rehabilitation-specific registry. Patients aged 15-65 years who completed the Swedish version of the BFI-2 were included. The five BFI-2 domains (extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, open-mindedness and negative emotionality) were analysed as continuous outcomes using multivariable linear regression with sex, age at injury or ACL reconstruction, body mass index (BMI), number of ACL injuries and preinjury Tegner activity level as predictors. Predominant personality trait groups were compared in a secondary exploratory analysis.
RESULTS: A total of 782 patients were included, of whom 692 had complete data for the regression analyses. Female sex was associated with higher scores in all five BFI-2 domains (all p ≤ 0.045). Older age was associated with higher extraversion, conscientiousness and open-mindedness and lower negative emotionality (all p ≤ 0.006). Higher BMI was associated with lower conscientiousness (p = 0.004) and higher open-mindedness (p = 0.049). The models explained 2.7%-13.0% of the variance in personality scores. In the secondary analysis, Agreeableness was the most common predominant trait, and patients classified as predominantly open-minded were older than patients in the other groups.
CONCLUSIONS: Sex and age were associated with several BFI-2 personality traits after ACL injury, whereas BMI showed only small associations. However, demographic characteristics explained little of the variance in personality scores, indicating that personality cannot be reliably inferred from demographic characteristics alone.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III.

title: Breast Injuries in Women's Rugby Union: A Comparison of Prospective and Retrospective Surveillance.
abstract: Retrospective research has reported a high prevalence of breast injuries in women's rugby union (RU); however, most injuries are not reported to medical staff. This study compared the incidence and severity of breast injuries collected both prospectively and retrospectively over a comparable match exposure period. Prospective surveillance was conducted by clinicians (n = 14) using an online injury surveillance system across 140 RU players. Retrospective surveillance was conducted using an anonymous online survey completed by 370 RU players. Injury incidence was calculated per 1000 hours of match exposure. Severity was assessed using breast pain, bruising and swelling, ability to continue play, perceived effect on performance, and long-term breast changes. Three breast injuries were prospectively recorded over 1204 hours of competition (2.5 injuries/1000 hours). In contrast, 144 breast injuries were reported retrospectively over 5055 hours of competition (28.5 injuries/1000 hours). The retrospective injury rate was significantly higher than the prospective rate (IRR = 11.4, 95% CI: 3.15-41.73; p < 0.002). Ninety-six percent (n = 139) of retrospectively reported injuries had not been disclosed to medical staff. Injury severity was similar between surveillance methods, with bruising commonly reported, all players continuing to participate despite injury, and over half perceiving a negative effect on performance. Long-term breast changes were reported by 6% (n = 8) of players. The substantially lower incidence recorded prospectively suggests that breast injuries are underreported in women's RU. Improved reporting and surveillance strategies are required to better capture breast injuries and support female athlete health and performance.

title: Efficacy and safety study of diclofenac epolamine topical patch in accelerating rehabilitation of moderate hamstring strain: A randomized controlled trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Moderate hamstring strain is a common sports injury impairing daily and athletic function. While topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) offer localized pain relief with reduced systemic effects, high-quality evidence specific to hamstring injury is limited.
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the effect of a short-course topical diclofenac epolamine patch combined with rehabilitation on pain and functional recovery in moderate hamstring strain.
METHODS: In this single-center, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 120 patients were randomized to an experimental group (diclofenac patch twice daily for 14 days plus rehabilitation) or a control group (placebo patch plus identical rehabilitation). Outcomes assessed included pain measured by the Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), as the primary endpoint, muscle strength, knee range of motion (ROM), functional back-kick test, time to rehabilitation criteria and safety (adverse events, liver/renal function).
RESULTS: The diclofenac group demonstrated significantly greater pain reduction at days 14, 21 and 28 post-intervention (all p < 0.01). Muscle strength recovery was superior at days 21 and 28, knee ROM improved more at day 28 and functional back-kick performance was better at day 28 (all p < 0.05). Time to meet rehabilitation criteria was significantly shorter in the experimental group (p = 0.002). Adverse event incidence and changes in liver/renal function were similar between groups (all p > 0.05).
CONCLUSION: A short-course topical diclofenac epolamine patch, combined with rehabilitation training, effectively alleviates pain, accelerates functional recovery, and is safe for treating moderate hamstring strain, supporting its use in clinical and sports rehabilitation.

title: Effects of caffeine supplementation on exercise-induced muscle damage: A systematic review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD) commonly occurs following unaccustomed or high-intensity exercise and is characterized by delayed-onset muscle soreness, elevated muscle damage biomarkers, and transient declines in muscle function. Caffeine, a widely consumed ergogenic aid, has been proposed to mitigate these adverse effects; however, the evidence across studies remains equivocal. This systematic review aimed to synthesize findings from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that investigated the effects of caffeine supplementation on markers of EIMD.
METHODS: Following preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses guidelines, a comprehensive search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar databases, supplemented by citation tracking. RCTs published between 2005 and 2025 that included human participants and reported direct or indirect indicators of EIMD were eligible. Fifteen RCTs (n = 222) were included and assessed for methodological quality using the PEDro scale.
RESULTS: Caffeine doses ranged from 3 to 6 mg/kg. Among the 6 studies assessing delayed-onset muscle soreness, 4 reported significant reductions in perceived soreness within 24 to 48 hours post-exercise, whereas 2 found no effect or adverse responses. Eleven studies examined biochemical markers; most detected no significant differences between caffeine and placebo, while 2 observed higher creatine kinase levels in the caffeine group. Five studies evaluated functional performance; some indicated attenuation of decrements in maximal voluntary isometric contraction or isokinetic torque, although results were inconsistent.
CONCLUSION: Caffeine supplementation may transiently reduce subjective muscle soreness and, under certain conditions, help preserve muscle function following EIMD, but its effects on biochemical markers are inconsistent. The overall efficacy appears to depend on factors such as exercise modality, dosage, timing, and inter-individual variability. Larger, well-controlled RCTs with standardized protocols are needed to clarify caffeine's role in muscle damage and recovery.

title: Prospective Polynomial Characterization of Tibial Plateau Geometry Shows No Association With Contralateral ACL Injury in Female Athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries are common in athletic people, with young female athletes at particularly high risk. After ACL injury, reconstruction, and return to sport, many sustain contralateral ACL (CACL) injuries. While tibial plateau cartilage surface geometry has been associated with first-time ACL injury risk, its role in subsequent CACL injury remains unclear.
HYPOTHESIS: The normal knee of female athletes who suffered a first-time ACL injury, underwent reconstruction, returned to preinjury activities and subsequently suffered a CACL injury will have tibial plateau cartilage surface geometry that is different compared with an equivalent population who did not sustain a subsequent CACL injury.
STUDY DESIGN: Prospective cohort study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 2.
METHODS: A total of 199 subjects who suffered a first-time ACL injury, had reconstruction, returned to preinjury activities and had a contralateral knee that was normal underwent bilateral magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan acquisitions. Tibial plateau cartilage geometry was assessed on the uninjured, normal knees using T1-weighted Fast Field Echo MRI. Parasagittal slices at maximum cartilage concavity in medial and lateral compartments of the tibia were characterized by fitting fifth-order polynomials. Female athletes who sustained a CACL injury within 4 years of reconstruction and return to sport (n = 12) were matched and compared with a group of female athletes who did not sustain CACL injury (n = 24). Random coefficient mixed-effects regression was used to assess group differences in polynomial functions.
RESULTS: No significant differences in tibial cartilage surface geometry were found between the first-time ACL and first-time ACL + CACL injury groups in the medial (P = 0.23) and lateral (P = 0.18) compartments.
CONCLUSION: These findings suggest that characterization of tibial plateau cartilage geometry in the normal knee of subjects who underwent reconstruction after a first-time ACL injury is insufficient to predict who will on go on to suffer a subsequent CACL injury.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: More comprehensive predictive models incorporating anatomic, biomechanical, and psychological factors are likely needed to identify those at increased risk for CACL injury after a first-time ACL injury and reconstruction.

title: Effectiveness of a Structured Post-Platelet Rich Plasma Rehabilitation Approach on Pain and Function in Subacromial Pain Syndrome: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Subacromial pain syndrome (SAPS) causes pain and functional limitation. Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP) is increasingly used as a supportive treatment. Optimal rehabilitation after PRP is unclear. This study investigated the effectiveness of a structured post-PRP rehabilitation approach on pain and function.
METHODS: Sixty participants with SAPS were randomized to two groups; 54 completed the study and were included in the final per-protocol analysis (27 per group). During a 21-day period, the study group received a structured post-PRP rehabilitation approach in addition to standard conventional physiotherapy, while the control group received standard conventional physiotherapy alone. Range of motion, muscle strength, and posture were evaluated. In addition, outcome measures included the Short-Form McGill Pain Questionnaire (SF-MPQ), Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand Questionnaire (DASH), Functional Impairment Test-Hand and Neck/Shoulder/Arm (FIT-HaNSA) and Constant-Murley Shoulder Score, which were administered for assessment purposes.
RESULTS: Corbin Posture Scale scores decreased in both groups (p < 0.05). Pain reduction was greater in the study group (VAS: from 9.00 ± 0.67 to 2.92 ± 1.14 versus from 9.11 ± 0.64 to 7.96 ± 0.75; SF-MPQ: from 27.07 ± 4.41 to 10.07 ± 3.33 versus from 21.33 ± 2.46 to 19.37 ± 2.35; p < 0.001). Improvements in Constant-Murley, DASH, and FIT-HaNSA scores, shoulder muscle strength, and active and passive range of motion were significantly greater in the study group (p < 0.001).
DISCUSSION: Adding a structured post-PRP rehabilitation approach to standard conventional physiotherapy may provide additional short-term improvements in pain, muscle strength, range of motion, and shoulder function compared with standard conventional physiotherapy alone in individuals with SAPS. However, long-term follow-up was not conducted. Therefore, the sustainability of the observed improvements remains unclear. Future studies should investigate the long-term effects of structured post-PRP rehabilitation approaches.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT07410208; registered on January 21, 2026.
