title: Return-to-Play Outcomes After Primary Ulnar Collateral Ligament Reconstruction Vary Substantially Depending on Return Criteria: A Systematic Review Stratified by Competition Level.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To determine how return definitions influence return to play (RTP), return to the same level of play (RTSP), advancement rates, and return timelines after primary ulnar collateral ligament reconstruction (UCLR) in baseball pitchers across levels of competition.
METHODS: Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines, PubMed and Embase were searched from January 2000 to January 2025. Studies evaluating baseball pitchers undergoing primary UCLR and reporting RTP, RTSP, advancement, or return timing outcomes with participation-based (RTP based on a single event) or durability-based (RTP after sustained participation over a predefined threshold) criteria were included. Primary outcomes were RTP, RTSP, and advancement rate (progression to a higher level after UCLR); secondary outcome was return time stratified by return criteria. Risk of bias was assessed with the Methodological Index for Non-randomized Studies and Risk Of Bias in Non-randomized Studies of Interventions tools.
RESULTS: Twenty-four studies met inclusion. Across these studies, 19 included Major League Baseball players (2194 players), 5 included Minor League Baseball (MiLB) players (2318 players), 4 included collegiate athletes (553 athletes), and 6 included high school athletes (258 athletes). RTP/RTSP rates were 86% to 92%/70% to 87% in high school, 84%/67% to 92% in college, 76.3% to 79%/69.1% to 100% in MiLB, and 80% to 97.2%/28.1% to 87% in Major League Baseball. Advancement was 55.7% to 63.2% in high school, 4.1% to 44.4% in college, and 22.3% to 45% in MiLB. Surgery-to-return time using the common RTSP definition ranged from 13.7 to 20.5 months (Major League Baseball), 14.6 to 16.4 (MiLB), and 11 to 17 (college and high school). Durability-based definitions were not consistently associated with longer return intervals.
CONCLUSIONS: Without standardized return criteria, reported RTP, RTSP, advancement rates, and return timelines after primary UCLR in baseball pitchers varied substantially across studies and competition levels. Durability-based criteria were not consistently associated with longer return timelines, indicating that return outcomes should be interpreted according to the competition level and return definition used. Standardized, tier-specific return criteria may improve clinical interpretation after primary UCLR.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV, systematic review of Level II to IV studies.

title: Effects of Oral L-Arginine on Everyday Persistent Fatigue, Sleep, and Post-Exercise Lactate Recovery in Community-Dwelling Working-Age Adults: A Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Randomized Trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: The evidence for nutritional interventions against fatigue is limited; we evaluated whether L-arginine reduces fatigue in working-age adults.
METHODS: In this 8-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 120 community-dwelling working-age adults aged 30-59 years with persistent fatigue (Fatigue Severity Scale [FSS] total ≥ 27) received oral L-arginine 3 g/day, 6 g/day, or placebo. The primary endpoint was FSS change; secondary endpoints included the Checklist Individual Strength (CIS), Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and blood lactate kinetics during a standardized submaximal treadmill run (~70% VO2max, 30 min). Data from 119 participants were analyzed, with Holm adjustment for multiplicity.
RESULTS: At Week 8, FSS decreased more with 6 g/day than with placebo (-6.41 vs. -2.23; Holm-adjusted p = 0.024), whereas 3 g/day did not differ from placebo. The 6 g/day CIS improvement did not survive multiplicity adjustment. PSQI scores improved nominally at both doses (3 g/day, p = 0.007; 6 g/day, p = 0.045). With 6 g/day, the total lactate area under the curve (Holm-adjusted p = 0.041) and 15-min recovery lactate (Holm-adjusted p = 0.002) were lower than with the placebo, whereas the resting plasma nitrite did not differ. No serious adverse events occurred.
CONCLUSIONS: L-arginine supplementation at 6 g/day for 8 weeks reduced fatigue severity relative to placebo and was well-tolerated; however, mean FSS scores remained above the enrollment threshold, indicating a reduction in, rather than resolution of, persistent fatigue.

title: Orthobiologics for hand and wrist disorders: An indication-specific systematic review and evidence-gap synthesis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Orthobiologics are increasingly used in hand and wrist disorders; however, their clinical effectiveness remains uncertain due to heterogeneity in indications, formulations, and outcome reporting.
METHODS: This systematic review was reported in accordance with PRISMA 2020 and prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261359867). PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, and Web of Science were searched from inception through March 31, 2026. Primary clinical studies evaluating locally delivered orthobiologics for hand or wrist disorders were eligible. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2 for randomized trials and ROBINS-I for nonrandomized comparative studies and the Joanna Briggs Institute checklist for uncontrolled case series; certainty was evaluated using GRADE. Because the studies differed substantially in indication, biologic formulation, comparator, follow-up, and outcome definition, meta-analysis was not clinically appropriate; a structured qualitative synthesis was performed.
RESULTS: Ten primary clinical studies were included: three studies of carpal tunnel syndrome, one of de Quervain tenosynovitis, three of trapeziometacarpal osteoarthritis, one of distal-radius fracture, and two of scaphoid nonunion. No meta-analysis was performed. Evidence for carpal tunnel syndrome was inconsistent across comparators and follow-up durations. In de Quervain tenosynovitis, PRP produced outcomes comparable to corticosteroid injection, with fewer reported local adverse effects. Evidence for trapeziometacarpal osteoarthritis was limited and comparator-dependent. In scaphoid nonunion, the primary BMP studies suggested possible osteoinductive benefit but also identified complications, including heterotopic ossification, persistent nonunion, and reoperation. Overall certainty ranged from moderate to very low.
CONCLUSIONS: Orthobiologic effectiveness for hand and wrist disorders appears indication-specific but is supported by limited and heterogeneous evidence. Routine PRP use in osteoarthritis is not supported, and application in other conditions should remain selective and context-dependent. Larger, adequately powered, placebo-controlled trials with standardized biologic characterization and outcome reporting are required. These findings should be interpreted as an evidence-gap map rather than proof of comparative efficacy.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV (systematic review of predominantly small randomized and nonrandomized studies with heterogeneous designs and limited sample sizes).

title: A Study of Functional Outcome of Arthroscopic Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Using Hamstring Graft.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury is a common cause of knee instability and functional limitation. Arthroscopic reconstruction using hamstring tendon autografts is widely used because of favorable functional outcomes and lower donor-site morbidity.
AIM: This study aims to evaluate the clinical and functional outcomes of patients undergoing arthroscopic ACL reconstruction using a hamstring tendon autograft.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: A prospective observational study was conducted over 18 months in the Department of Orthopaedics, M.G.M. Medical College and L.S.K. Hospital, Kishanganj, Bihar. Fifty patients aged 18-50 years with clinically and radiologically confirmed ACL tears underwent primary arthroscopic ACL reconstruction using a quadrupled hamstring tendon autograft. Femoral fixation was performed using a cortical button and tibial fixation using an interference screw. Patients were followed at 1, 2, 3, 6, and 12 months. Functional outcome was assessed using the Lysholm Knee Scoring Scale, while clinical stability and post-operative complications were documented. No comparator group was included. The study was confined to one institution, and no instrumented laxity measurements or formal return-to-sport outcomes were reported.
RESULTS: The mean age of participants was 31.72 ± 8.88 years, and 72% were male. Road traffic accidents were the commonest mechanism of injury (44%), followed by sports-related injuries (36%). Medial meniscal tear was the most common associated injury (40%). Fifteen of 50 patients (30%) experienced a recorded post-operative complication. In the total cohort, anterior knee pain occurred in 5/50 (10%), tunnel widening in 4/50 (8%), infection in 3/50 (6%), and tibial screw dislodgement, graft failure, and knee stiffness in 1/50 (2%) each. The mean Lysholm score improved from 50.74 ± 6.342 preoperatively to 86.00 ± 10.067 postoperatively (P < 0.05); 52% had good, and 32% had excellent Lysholm outcomes at final follow-up.
CONCLUSION: In this single-center prospective observational cohort of 50 patients, Lysholm scores improved over 12 months after hamstring autograft ACL reconstruction, with 84% classified as having good-to-excellent outcomes. These findings describe short-term recovery within the treated cohort. The absence of a comparator and adjusted analyses precludes causal attribution or conclusions about superiority over alternative reconstruction strategies or non-operative management; long-term effectiveness and return to sport were not established.

title: Musculoskeletal Health in Elite Athletes With Bilateral Lower Limb Loss: The ADVANCE Cohort Study.
abstract:
CONTEXT: Lower limb (LL) loss can be detrimental to bone and joint health. Exercise improves musculoskeletal outcomes in individuals without LL loss, but with limited investigation after LL loss. The aim is to assess differences in bone and joint health between elite athletes and nonathletes with bilateral LL loss to assess associations between exercise and musculoskeletal health in this population.
DESIGN: ADVANCE (Armed Services Trauma Rehabilitation Outcome) is a longitudinal cohort study involving UK military personnel and veterans who served in Afghanistan.
METHODS: Sixty-four ambulatory participants with bilateral LL loss were included. Seven participants were elite athletes (athlete group; n = 7) and were compared with the remaining participants (nonathlete group, n = 57). The Kellgren-Lawrence score for knee and hip osteoarthritis (OA), femoral neck and lumbar spine bone mineral density (BMD), Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score, Non-Arthritic Hip Score, International Physical Activity Questionnaire, and 6-minute walk test distance were compared. Outcomes were also compared between the Athlete group and Nonathlete group split by activity level.
RESULTS: Participants were 33.1 ± 4.7 years old and 6.9 ± 1.5 years postinjury. No Athlete group participants had knee OA compared with 51.8% of Nonathlete participants. There was a weak trend for more prevalent hip OA in the Nonathlete group (P = .074); 7.1% Athlete group participants and 30.7% Nonathlete group participants had Kellgren-Lawrence score ≥ 1. Femoral neck BMD was not different between groups, but there was a trend for lower lumbar spine BMD in the Nonathlete group compared with the Athlete group (-0.41 vs 0.57; P = .06). More active nonathletes had better femoral neck t scores than less active nonathletes, P = .03. Neither Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score Pain, Symptoms, Non-Arthritic Hip Score, nor 6-minute walk test distance were different between groups.
CONCLUSION: Athletes and active nonathletes with LL loss may have favorable BMD profiles. Athletes with LL loss have lower prevalence of radiographic hip and knee OA. Although not conclusive due to our study design, this suggests that exercise may be associated with beneficial musculoskeletal health outcomes in this population.

title: Age-Related Patterns of Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs) Symptoms and Key Performance Factors in Adolescent Biathletes.
abstract: Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs) impairs health and performance, but age-related patterns in its emergence remain unclear. This study examines RED symptoms in adolescent biathletes at season-start and their link to end-of-season performance. A national cross-sectional study including prospective performance registration recruited biathletes to complete validated questionnaires, followed by clinical interviews if eating disorders (EDs) were indicated. Athletes ≥ 18 years were invited for physical laboratory assessments. End-of-season results were retrieved from open records. Analyses were performed by elastic net regression to identify the most stable predictors of performance, which were finally included in a linear regression model. Seventy-two athletes (55% females) with mean (SD) age 17.8 (1.4) years, 13.3 (3.3) training hours/week, and representing median (min, max) tier 3.0 (2, 5) were included. Prevalence in symptoms of low energy availability (LEA) was 18%, REDs 32%, EDs 11% (20% among females), and of depression 15%. Among 28 athletes (43% female) completing laboratory assessments, 11% had low BMD and ≤ 25% had clinical metabolic markers. Symptoms of mental health issues and REDs were more common in females and the older age groups. Higher training volume and low RED severity positively predicted performance, whereas injury/illness-related training absences, cholesterol, and body fat percentage negatively affected race results. RED symptoms are common in young biathletes. Illness/injury-related training absences were frequent and linked to poorer end-of-season performance, underscoring the need for routine screening by health- and performance teams to detect and manage early symptoms of LEA, reduce RED risk, and prevent premature career termination.

title: Investigation of reaction time in children with brachial plexus birth injuries: A controlled study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Brachial plexus birth injury (BPBI) results in musculoskeletal impairments, sensory deficits, and central nervous system alterations that may negatively affect upper extremity function; however, reaction time (RT), which reflects sensorimotor integration, central information processing, and motor response generation, has not been comprehensively investigated in children with BPBI.
PURPOSE: The aim was to compare upper extremity reaction time between the affected and unaffected sides in children with BPBI and healthy controls while examining its relationships with upper extremity performance, sensation, bilateral coordination, balance, activity, participation, and fall frequency.
STUDY DESIGN: Cross-sectional case-control study.
METHODS: Seventy-six children with upper trunk BPBI and 72 healthy controls were included. Reaction time was assessed using BlazePod. Active movements were evaluated using the Active Movement Scale (AMS), upper extremity performance with the Box and Block Test (BBT), sensation with the Semmes-Weinstein Monofilament Test, bilateral coordination and balance with the Bruininks Oseretsky Motor Proficiency Test, activity and participation with the Pediatric Outcomes Data Collection Instrument.
RESULTS: Reaction time was longer on the affected side (555.3±89.5 ms) than the unaffected side (495.9±73.7 ms) and healthy controls (476.2±71.7 ms) (p<0.001). Reaction time showed a strong negative correlation with BBT (r=-0.72, p<0.001), a moderate negative correlation with bilateral coordination (r=-0.51, p<0.001), and a moderate positive correlation with sensation (r=0.42, p<0.001). Weak negative correlations were noted for AMS (r=-0.31, p<0.05) and activity and participation (r=-0.26, p<0.05); however, balance showed no correlation (p=0.12). Children with BPBI had a higher fall frequency than healthy controls (p<0.001), and fall frequency was not associated with reaction time (p>0.05).
CONCLUSIONS: RT is prolonged in the affected extremity in children with BPBI and may negatively affect upper extremity performance and bilateral coordination. Incorporating RT-oriented interventions into rehabilitation may enhance functional and sports performance in children with BPBI.

title: Efficacy of Apparent Diffusion Coefficient Sampling in Muscle Tears and Intersex Differences in Professional Football Players: A Cohort Study.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the gold standard for monitoring the evolution of muscle injuries in athletes, although no established quantitative measure of recovery currently exists.
HYPOTHESIS: Apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) values may provide a quantitative measure of muscle healing, and sex-related differences may exist in the evolution of muscle injuries.
STUDY DESIGN: Single-center retrospective observational cohort study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 2a.
METHODS: Twenty-six professional football (soccer) players (13 male ,13 female) undergoing MRI for muscle injury were retrospectively selected between October 2020 and June 2024. All athletes underwent MRI at baseline (T0) and at 2-week follow-up, including diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) acquisitions with b values of 0-100-800 s/mm². Two musculoskeletal radiologists measured ADC values within the index lesions at each examination. Changes in ADC between the two time points (ΔADC) were assessed using a paired-samples t test, while sex-related differences were evaluated using the Mann-Whitney U test.
RESULTS: The overall mean ADC value at the lesion site decreased from 2.06 ± 0.35 mm2/s at T0 to 1.61 ± 0.30 mm2/s at follow-up corresponding to a mean ΔADC of 0.44 ± 0.20 and a 21.84% reduction. The difference between T0 and follow-up was statistically significant (t = 8.12; P < 0.001). Mean ΔADC values were 0.32 ± 0.20 mm²/s in male players and 0.56 ± 0.25 mm²/s in female players, respectively, with a statistically significant difference between sexes (z = -2.95; P = 0.003). When only hamstring injuries were considered, female players showed a significantly greater decrease in ADC over time than male players (Mann-Whitney U test; exact P = 0.02), with mean ΔADC values of 0.56 ± 0.30 and 0.26 ± 0.08 mm²/s, respectively.
CONCLUSION: Muscle injury is associated with an acute increase in ADC values followed by a progressive decrease during healing. ADC may therefore represent a quantitative imaging biomarker for monitoring muscle recovery.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: ADC measurement within muscle tears may provide a quantitative assessment of healing status and support individualized rehabilitation strategies in athletes. Sex-related differences may exist in injury pathophysiology and recovery patterns relevant to safe return to play.

title: Thumb muscle activation with task-specific exercise: A pilot study with participant self-report implementation outcomes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Thumb carpometacarpal osteoarthritis is a common source of pain, weakness, and reduced hand function and upper extremity rehabilitation. Although isometric stabilization exercises are commonly used in hand therapy to support dynamic thumb carpometacarpal control, limited task-specific evidence guides exercise selection.
PURPOSE: To examine muscle activation across four isometric thumb-hand positions in healthy adults and describe participant perceptions of the protocol's acceptability, feasibility, and appropriateness before testing in symptomatic hand therapy samples.
STUDY DESIGN: Cross-sectional, within-subject repeated-measures pilot study.
METHODS: Seven healthy right-handed adults (mean age, 22.7 ± 0.48 years) performed four submaximal isometric exercise conditions at approximately 80% perceived effort: composite finger-thumb squeeze, "bunny-ears" pinch, resisted index-finger abduction, and fingertip-only press. Surface electromyography was recorded from the abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis, first dorsal interosseous, and forearm flexor group. Integrated electromyography was normalized within participants to each muscle's maximum response across conditions. A two-way repeated-measures analysis of variance (condition × muscle) compared normalized activation. Participants rated acceptability, feasibility, and appropriateness on five-point Likert scales.
RESULTS: Normalized activation differed by muscle, F(3,18) = 14.22, p < 0.001, ηp² = 0.70, with a significant condition × muscle interaction, F(9,54) = 7.29, p < 0.001, ηp² = 0.55. Abductor pollicis brevis activation was highest during composite squeeze and bunny-ears pinch (0.93 ± 0.05 and 0.85 ± 0.06) and lowest during resisted index-finger abduction (0.31 ± 0.07). Opponens pollicis activation was highest during composite squeeze and resisted index-finger abduction (0.79 ± 0.07 and 0.75 ± 0.09). Mean construct-based ratings of acceptability, feasibility, and appropriateness ranged from 4.54-4.79 out of 5.
CONCLUSIONS: Findings provide preliminary evidence to inform hand therapy exercise selection by showing that functional isometric thumb-hand positions produce distinct intrinsic and extrinsic activation profiles. Favorable participant perceptions support protocol refinement and testing in larger and symptomatic hand therapy samples.

title: Discriminant and Prognostic Validity of the Multimodal Exertional Test (MET) for Athletes with Concussion.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Exertional tests have become an informative tool to assist with clinical concussion management and return-to-sport medical decisions. However, current tests are resource intensive and thus, we developed a widely accessible, multimodal exertional test (MET). The objectives of this study were: (1) To evaluate the discriminant validity of the MET by examining sex-stratified differences in symptoms, heart rate (HR), and performance metrics between concussed and healthy athletes; and (2) To assess the predictive (prognostic) validity of the MET by determining whether week 1 MET performance predicts time to medical clearance.
METHODS: This study was conducted at a single academic institution and affiliated sport medicine clinic in Toronto, Canada, with participants recruited between August 2022 and November 2024. 115 interuniversity athletes (female n=49, male n=66) completed the MET at off-season and 55 interuniversity athletes with concussion (female n=37, male n=18) completed the MET up to six times at 1-, 2-, 3-, 4-, 6-, and 8-weeks post-injury. Average and maximum HR, symptoms, performance metrics, and MET pass/fail status were measured prior to and during the protocol. Probabilistic hierarchical models were implemented to estimate differences between concussion and healthy athletes (discriminant validity) and negative binomial analyses were used to examine whether MET performance predicted time to medical clearance (predictive validity).
RESULTS: At 1-week post injury, concussed athletes exhibited greater symptom provocation during the MET compared to healthy athletes, with differences after each task. MET failure rates were highest during weeks 1 (63%) and 2 (49%) and declined through week 8. Athletes who passed the MET at week 1 recovered 20.6 days faster (90% Credible Interval [CrI] = 4.9-36.8 days, posterior probability [pprob] > 0 = 97.7%) than those who failed.
CONCLUSION: The MET demonstrates discriminant validity by eliciting greater symptom provocation in athletes with concussion compared to healthy athletes. Improvements in symptoms and completion rates over 8 weeks indicate recovery-related gains in exertional tolerance. The MET also demonstrates predictive validity, as passing the test at week 1 was associated with faster time to medical clearance, supporting its potential utility as an early prognostic tool in concussion management.

title: Horizontal and Multidirectional Single-Leg Hop Tests Predict Isokinetic Quadriceps and Hamstring Strengths After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: After anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR), isokinetic strength and single-leg hop tests (SLHT) are used to assess return to sport readiness. This study examined the relationships and predictive effects of isokinetic knee extension (Ex) and flexion (Flx) strength with 5 SLHTs at 6 to 8 months post-ACLR.
HYPOTHESIS: There would be significant correlation between knee Ex and Flx strengths on the operated side and 5 different SLHTs; SLHTs would significantly predict knee isokinetic Ex and Flx strength.
STUDY DESIGN: Cross-sectional study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 3.
METHODS: Fifty-one male participants underwent unilateral ACLR. Lysholm, International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC), and Tegner scales were assessed preoperatively and 6 to 8 months postoperatively. At the same follow-up, isokinetic strength at 60°/s, 180°/s, and 240°/s and 5 SLHTs were tested on both limbs. Data were analyzed with paired t tests, Pearson correlations, Fisher's exact test, and simple linear regression; limb symmetry index (LSI) cut-off was ≥85%.
RESULTS: Isokinetic strength and single-leg hop (SH), crossover hop, and medial side triple-hop (TH) distances did not differ significantly between limbs (P > 0.05), whereas TH and 90° medial rotation hop distances were significantly shorter on the operated side (P < 0.05). Participants' Lysholm and IKDC scores improved significantly at 6 to 8 months post-ACLR (P < 0.001), but Tegner activity level did not change significantly (P > 0.05). High correlation was found between Ex strength at 60°/s and SH and TH distances on the operated side, and high-moderate correlations were found at 180°/s and 240°/s. Flx strengths showed a similar but slightly lower degree of correlation. Simple linear regression models revealed that especially SH and TH distances significantly predicted both Ex and Flx strengths (adjusted R2 0.26-0.52; P < 0.001). Among the LSI values, only a significant correlation was found between 60°/s Ex and TH LSI ratio (P = 0.01).
CONCLUSION: The findings show that SH and TH tests were highly predictive of isokinetic knee strength after ACLR.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: SLHTs after ACLR can be used as a practical and accessible complement to isokinetic measurements.

title: Athletes and Medical Staff in Elite Contact Sports: a Quantitative Analysis of Use, Knowledge, and Attitudes Regarding Cannabinoids.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cannabis use among elite contact sport athletes increases with legal reform and commercial availability. Limited education in cannabinoid pharmacology, use, and risk persists among athletes and medical staff, fostering stigma and reducing evidence-based guidance and communication.
HYPOTHESIS: Athletes use cannabis but perceive stigma and discomfort discussing cannabis with medical staff.
STUDY DESIGN: Quantitative, descriptive cross-sectional surveys.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 4.
METHODS: Two anonymous online surveys were administered to elite and professional contact sport athletes (Canada, United States, Australia) and medical and training staff (February 2023 to July 2024). Descriptive statistics assessed demographics, use patterns, knowledge, education needs, attitudes, stigma, communication, and league policies.
RESULTS: A total of 166 athletes (89.7% male, 35.2% aged 18-23 years) and 64 medical staff (physicians, athletic therapists, strength and conditioning coaches, etc) responded. Knowledge (pharmacology, interactions, dosing) was low. Overall, 56% of athletes currently used cannabinoids (81% having ever used), but only 21.7% knew the endocannabinoid system and 67.4% were unfamiliar with therapeutic dosing. Among medical staff, 59.5% were unfamiliar with mechanisms, only 14% were familiar with dosing protocols, and 71.4% lacked confidence in making treatment plans. Of the athletes, 86.5% believed cannabis had therapeutic value, 72.3% wanted education, and 74.1% favored qualified scientists as instructors. Of the medical staff, 79.5% reported strong educational need, with 100% of staff desiring athlete-specific cannabinoid education. Stigma and communication barriers were substantial: 81.3% of athletes perceived public stigma, 66.1% perceived staff stigma, and only 21.4% felt comfortable discussing cannabis with medical staff. Staff believed athletes would be honest if approached; however, <50% believed athletes trusted them enough to start the conversation. Both athletes and medical staff categorized cannabinoids as supplements or medications (unlike street drugs) and both supported legalization and a revision and update on league cannabis policies.
CONCLUSION: Athletes and medical staff exhibit parallel knowledge gaps and strong educational needs amid high interest, use, and significant communication barriers. Evidence-informed education and stigma-reducing strategies are urgently needed.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Athletes increasingly use cannabinoids for pain, sleep, and recovery, while medical staff report insufficient training and low confidence. System-level education, communication, and policy updates may improve safety, decision-making, and trust.

title: Warning signs of Injury: Changes in pain, training load, and wellness in elite youth athletes.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Examine week-by-week changes during the four weeks preceding injury compared with injury-free weeks.
DESIGN: Prospective study.
SETTING: and main outcome: Training load was calculated as (weekly training minutes x average weekly rate of perceived exertion)/1000 (sRPE). Pain was assessed with a rating scale 0-10. Wellness (sleep, fatigue, stress and mental recovery) were standardized using Z-scores. Injury was self-reported.
PARTICIPANTS: Elite youth athletes.
RESULTS: Among 146 athletes, 118 (80.8%) reported 125 injuries. Mean age was 17.0 (SD 0.8). Compared with injury-free weeks, significantly higher pain scores were observed one (md [IQR]: 2.0 [0.0-4.0], p = 0.039) and two weeks (2.0 [1.0-3.0], p = 0.047) prior to injury. Median sRPE was significantly lower three (md [IQR]: 2.30 [0.75-4.20], p = 0.012) and four weeks (2.40 [0.96-3.96], p = 0.011). Sleep, stress and total wellness were significantly lower one week (mean [SD]: -0.348 [1.1], p = 0.004; -0.272 [0.9], p = 0.017; -0.244 [1.0], p = 0.011), while stress also showed reduction two weeks prior to injury (-0.244 [1.0], p = 0.042).
CONCLUSION: Changes were observed mainly in the week preceding injury. Increased pain and reduced wellness may serve as early warning signs, while decreased training load may reflect adaptation rather than causation. These findings support injury as a progressive process with detectable warning signs.

title: Musculoskeletal injury patterns and factors associated with anatomical injury location among surveyed padel players in Saudi Arabia: A cross-sectional study.
abstract: BackgroundPadel is a growing sport in Saudi Arabia; however, data on related musculoskeletal injuries and associated factors are limited. The increasing number of players highlights the importance of understanding padel-related injury patterns and their associated characteristics.ObjectiveTo describe self-reported musculoskeletal injury patterns among surveyed padel players in Saudi Arabia and examine player-, exposure-, equipment-, and injury-related characteristics associated with anatomical injury location among reported injury cases.MethodA cross-sectional study was conducted using a self-administered questionnaire distributed through convenience and snowball sampling to padel players in Saudi Arabia between February and March 2025. The questionnaire collected information on demographic characteristics, playing exposure, equipment characteristics, injury history, and injury-related characteristics.ResultsA total of 600 padel players were included in the analysis, of whom 301 reported at least one padel-related musculoskeletal injury, corresponding to 50.2% of the surveyed sample, with 513 reported injury cases. Upper-quadrant injuries were the most frequently reported (44.1%), followed by foot/ankle (22.4%), spine (18.5%), and knee injuries (15.0%). In multivariable GEE analyses of reported injury observations, weekly playing hours were associated with foot/ankle and knee injury classification. Other significant associations with anatomical injury classification involved ADL limitation, pain severity, recovery duration, recurrence, sex, padel education, and racket hardness, with patterns varying by anatomical location.ConclusionThese findings characterize self-reported musculoskeletal injury patterns among surveyed padel players and identify characteristics associated with anatomical injury location. Prospective studies are needed to determine factors associated with subsequent injury occurrence and to inform targeted preventive strategies.

title: Bone Mineral Density in Physique-Focused and Non-Physique-Focused Female Collegiate Athletes: Associations With Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport Risk Factors.
abstract: Kolb, DE, Cipriano, NL, Moody, RA, Stephens, JA, Caldwell, LK, Lindley, MR, Ware, ME, and Deemer, SE. Bone mineral density in physique-focused and non-physique-focused female collegiate athletes: Associations with relative energy deficiency in sport risk factors. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Bone mineral density (BMD) is a critical indicator of skeletal health and long-term injury risk in athletic populations. Female athletes are susceptible to changes in BMD because of sport-specific training demands, hormonal dysregulation, and energy availability. The present study aimed to compare BMD between physique-focused (PF; endurance, aesthetic, and weight-dependent sports) and non-physique-focused (NPF; ball, power, and skill-based sports) female collegiate athletes and assess risk factors associated with relative energy deficiency in sport (REDs) across both groups. Thirty-three female athletes were evaluated for BMD by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA), REDs risk using the Clinical Assessment Tool 2 (CAT2), anthropometric measurements, blood biomarkers, the Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire (EDE-Q), and the Low Energy Availability in Females Questionnaire (LEAF-Q). Group differences were assessed using independent t-tests with significance set at p < 0.05. Physique-focused athletes demonstrated significantly lower DXA-derived z-scores at anteroposterior spine, right and left femur, and total body sites than NPF athletes (p < 0.001). There were no differences in leptin (p = 0.35), cortisol (p = 0.16), vitamin D (p = 0.29), LEAF-Q total score (p = 0.72), or global EDE-Q score (p = 0.10). No group differences in CAT2 REDs risk were observed; thus, subjects were combined: 19 athletes were classified as "green;" 12 were "yellow;" and 2 were "orange." Lower BMD in PF athletes supports the importance of early screening and targeted interventions to support bone health. These findings suggest sport type may influence skeletal outcomes independent of traditional REDs indicators, emphasizing the need for sport-specific assessment strategies.

title: Low energy availability, disordered eating, exercise dependence, and injury prevalence in female CrossFit® athletes.
abstract: CrossFit® incorporates high-intensity, multimodal training with strong elements of community and competition. Despite known physical and psychological benefits, musculoskeletal injury prevalence ranges from 15 to 75%. Due to training demands, CrossFit® athletes may be at risk for low energy availability (LEA), disordered eating (DE), and exercise dependence (EXD), which may increase injury risk. Female CrossFit® participants (n = 198) completed an online survey including the Low Energy Availability in Females Questionnaire (LEAF-Q), Exercise Dependence Scale (EDS-21), and Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire (EDE-Q). Participants were classified as DE only, primary EXD, secondary EXD (DE + EXD), or control (no DE or EXD risk). Statistical significance was set at p ≤ 0.05. Overall, 37.8% of participants were at risk for LEA, 43.9% for DE, and 15.1% for EXD. Participants with secondary EXD had significantly (p < 0.001) higher EDE-Q global scores (3.9 ± 1.0) compared to primary EXD (1.4 ± 0.7) and control groups (1.0 ± 0.7). Additionally, 71.7% reported exercising despite injury, and 45.4% reported an injury within the past year. The prevalence of LEA, DE, and EXD was comparable to prior research; however, the high proportion of athletes continuing to train while injured suggests EXD-related behaviors may contribute to injury prevalence among CrossFit® athletes. These findings underscore the importance of early screening and education on adequate fueling and healthy training behaviors to support long-term health, performance, and injury prevention.

title: An Adaptive Knee Brace Is Associated With Improved Dynamic Stabilization Compared With a Standard Passive Brace in Anterior Cruciate Ligament-Deficient Men During a Functional Hop Task.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To compare the dynamic knee stabilization effects of an adaptive dynamic brace (ADB) with those of a standard passive brace in anterior cruciate ligament (ACL)-deficient men.
METHODS: ACL-deficient participants were included. The subjects performed 3 single-leg functional hop tests: drop jump, crossover hop, and 90° rotational hop. Each task was performed once while wearing the ADB and once while wearing a traditional passive brace. Three-dimensional kinematic data were collected using an 8-camera optoelectronic motion-capture system. Repeated-measures analysis of variance was used to evaluate the effects of brace condition and time. An a priori power analysis indicated that a minimum of 12 participants were required.
RESULTS: Twelve ACL-deficient participants were included (age: 30.2 ± 3.4 years; time since injury: 32 ± 6 months; ACL-Return to Sport after Injury score: 70 ± 3). No significant differences in knee flexion angles were observed between braces. Knee flexion during landing was significantly lower in the crossover hop compared with the drop jump and rotational hop tasks (P < .01). During the drop jump task, the ADB significantly reduced knee valgus angles (P < .01). In the crossover hop task, the ADB significantly reduced both knee valgus and rotational angles (P < .01). During the rotational hop task, a significant brace-by-time interaction was observed for knee valgus (P < .05) and rotational angles (P < .05).
CONCLUSIONS: The ADB showed improved dynamic stabilization particularly during high-risk landing and rotational movement compared with a standard passive brace.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The ADB may enhance the effectiveness of rehabilitation strategies in ACL-deficient individuals by improving dynamic knee stability during functional activities.

title: Effectiveness of Pelvic Floor Muscle Training in Women Soccer Players and Its Relationship With Quality of Life and Pelvic Floor Muscle Strength: A Randomized Controlled Pilot Study.
abstract: Sebastian-Rico, JM, Muñoz-Fernández, MJ, Martínez-Aranda, LM, Calvo-Lluch, Á, and Ortega-Becerra, M. Effectiveness of pelvic floor muscle training in women soccer players and its relationship with quality of life and pelvic floor muscle strength: a randomized controlled pilot study. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study investigated the effects of a 6-week pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) program on muscle strength, function, and the prevalence of related dysfunctions in professional female soccer players using a randomized controlled pilot study design. Twenty nulliparous professional soccer players from the Spanish professional league (2024-2025 season) were randomly assigned to an experimental group (n = 12) or a control group (n = 8). Assessments included anthropometric data, validated questionnaires (International Consultation on Incontinence Questionnaire-Short Form and Broome Pelvic Muscle Self-Efficacy Scale), clinical interviews, and physical examination using the PERFECT method and manometry. The intervention consisted of a 6-week supervised PFMT program (4 sessions/week, 30 minutes each) progressed through 4 phases: education, proprioception, strengthening, and functional integration. Results showed significant group × time interactions for pelvic floor self-efficacy (Broome Pelvic Muscle Self-Efficacy Scale), with scores in the PFMT group increasing by 48.8 and 59.6% (p < 0.05), representing large between-group effect sizes (d = 0.91-1.26). Pelvic floor muscle performance increased by 122.4% in the intervention group (d = 1.25), whereas no meaningful changes were observed in the control group. No adverse events were reported. In conclusion, a 6-week supervised PFMT program is an effective and safe intervention for professional female soccer players, significantly improving muscle function and self-efficacy. These findings support the integration of PFMT for both therapeutic and preventive purposes in elite, high-impact sports environments.

title: Age-related slowing of sensorimotor reaction time in masters track and field athletes.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Masters athletes offer a powerful model for understanding how lifelong training shapes age‑related changes in reaction time (RT), a key indicator of sensorimotor performance.
PURPOSE: This cross-sectional study examined RT in masters track and field athletes across age, sex, RT tasks of varying complexity, and event disciplines (endurance, power, sprint).
METHODS: A total of 182 competitors (82 females) from the 2025 World Masters Athletics Championships completed four RT tasks using a wireless light-based testing system.
RESULTS: RT increased progressively with age across all tasks, with the slowest responses consistently observed in athletes ≥80 years old. Female athletes demonstrated slower RT than males, and RT increased systematically with task complexity. Sprint athletes showed faster RT than endurance athletes overall, although event‑specific differences did not persist within age groups. Age was positively associated with RT in all tasks (r = 0.41-0.53), with similar correlation strengths between sexes. Quadratic age effects emerged selectively in male athletes for two-hand simple and step-choice tasks, suggesting accelerated slowing at older ages in tasks requiring greater motor coordination. Linear regression models indicated that RT increased by approximately 3.3-3.6 ms per year of age after adjusting for sex, task, and event discipline, while body composition variables were not significant predictors.
CONCLUSIONS: Although lifelong training is associated with better sensorimotor performance, slower RT remains evident in masters athletes, with consistent sex differences and minimal influence of event discipline.

title: Enhancing Sleep in NCAA Division I Athletes: A Study of Sleep Extension Feasibility.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sleep extension has been shown to improve varied aspects of athletic performance in collegiate athletes. Such studies have been conducted in small cohorts in controlled settings utilizing obsolete monitoring technology. The feasibility of sleep extension has not been evaluated in a broader cohort of collegiate athletes with modern monitoring technology.
HYPOTHESIS: Sleep extension may not be feasible in National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) Division I athletes.
STUDY DESIGN: Crossover study.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 3.
METHODS: Baseline sleep data were collected from NCAA Division I athletes (women's soccer, men's soccer, baseball, and football) during a 2-week period. Subjects were then instructed to extend their total sleep time to 10 hours per night for 2 weeks. All sleep baseline and extension data were collected in the offseason, remote from school examinations. WHOOP bands recorded all sleep metrics. Data were analyzed using paired-samples t tests and Wilcoxon signed rank tests.
RESULTS: A total of 50 subjects (14 female, 36 male) participated. The study compared total sleep time (hours) and sleep consistency (percent) - the stability of sleep-wake schedule over time, between baseline and sleep extension phases. Sample size varied for both metrics, ranging from 46 to 49 participants, respectively. There was a statistically significant increase in sleep consistency during the sleep extension phase (baseline, 60.09 ± 12.6%; extension, 64.42 ± 12.4%; P = 0.02). However, total sleep time showed no significant difference between the 2 phases (baseline, 7.63 ± 0.88 hours; extension, 7.51 ± 0.88 hours; P = 0.27).
CONCLUSION: Extension efforts improved sleep consistency but did not significantly impact total sleep time suggesting that a sleep extension intervention can enhance sleep consistency in NCAA Division I athletes but does not significantly impact total sleep time. Sleep extension may be challenging for collegiate athletes given the time-intensive demands of both academics and sports. While sleep extension may be feasible in professional sports, it does not appear to be so in the college setting.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: While the sleep extension intervention improved sleep consistency, it did not improve total sleep time, questioning the feasibility of sleep extension in collegiate sports.

title: Acute neurotrophic responses to a single bout of blood flow restriction and eccentric overload exercise in healthy older men.
abstract: Blood flow restriction training (BFRT) combines substantial metabolic stress with low mechanical loading, but its neurotrophic effects remain unclear. This study investigated the acute effects of BFRT and eccentric overload exercise (EOE) on neurotrophic biomarkers in healthy older men. Sixty-three healthy older men (60-78 years) were randomized to BFRT, EOE, or a non-exercising control group. Neurotrophic, metabolic, endothelial, and muscle damage biomarkers were measured before and after exercise. Responses were analyzed using repeated-measures ANOVA, Bonferroni-adjusted post hoc comparisons, and correlations. Significant time × group interactions were observed for plasma BDNF (p = 0.017, ηp2 = 0.151) and IL-6 (p = 0.001, ηp2 = 0.22), while a marginal time × group interaction was observed for serum IGF-1 (p = 0.050, ηp2 = 0.096). BFRT induced a significant increase in BDNF (mean change = 226.5 pg/mL, p = 0.006), with a greater change compared to CON (p = 0.014). IGF-1 increased significantly from baseline to 1 h post-exercise within the BFRT group (mean change = 29.2 ng/mL, p = 0.005); however, changes did not differ significantly between groups. IL-6 increased significantly following both BFRT (mean change = 8.26 pg/mL, p < 0.001) and EOE (mean change = 3.56 pg/mL, p = 0.013); however, the increase was greater only following BFRT compared to CON (p = 0.001), with no significant difference between BFRT and EOE (p = 0.123). BFRT elicited greater lactate accumulation than EOE and CON, and changes in BDNF correlated with changes in lactate (r = 0.367, p = 0.007). EOE elicited a greater CK increase than CON 48 h post-exercise, whereas syndecan-1 concentrations remained unchanged. Acute BFRT increased circulating BDNF and IGF-1 in healthy older men, and was accompanied by greater lactate accumulation, modest CK elevations, and no detectable increase in syndecan-1. The association between lactate and BDNF suggests that metabolic stress may contribute to the acute peripheral biomarker response; however, the neurological and clinical significance of these transient circulating changes remains to be established.

title: Cardiac autonomic and hemodynamic responses to two-stage cycling and post-exercise recovery with partial blood flow restriction in young males.
abstract:
PURPOSE: This study compared acute cardiovascular and cardiac autonomic responses during graded (two-stage) aerobic cycling and subsequent recovery performed with and without partial blood flow restriction (BFR).
METHODS: Fifteen young males completed two sessions in a crossover design (control vs. bilateral thigh BFR). Each session included rest, 5 min of cycling at 40% maximal power output (Pmax), 5 min at 60% Pmax, and 10 min of recovery; BFR was released immediately at exercise cessation. ECG and arterial blood pressure were recorded. RR interval, mean arterial blood pressure (MBP), HRV (lnRMSSD, lnSDNN, HF, LF, LF/HF), and composite indices of cardiac sympathetic and parasympathetic activity (SNS, PNS) were derived from 3-min segments at rest, exercise, and recovery. Heart rate recovery at 30, 60, and 120 s after exercise cessation (HRR30, HRR60, HRR120) was calculated. Two-way repeated-measures ANOVA tested condition, time, and interaction.
RESULTS: Time × condition interactions were observed for RR interval (p=0.015) and MBP (p=0.003), indicating altered hemodynamic kinetics under BFR, primarily during recovery. HRV indices showed no time × condition interactions; however, BFR produced lower lnRMSSD, lnSDNN, HF, and PNS and higher SNS than control (all p<0.05), whereas LF and LF/HF were unchanged. HRR30 (p=0.040), HRR60 (p<0.001), and HRR120 (p=0.010) were attenuated under BFR.
CONCLUSIONS: BFR modifies cardiovascular regulation during two-stage cycling and recovery and induces sustained autonomic shifts toward reduced parasympathetic and increased sympathetic modulation, largely independent of exercise intensity. Altered recovery kinetics following cuff release highlight the importance of careful monitoring during the recovery phase when applying BFR.

abstract: Vatne, EA, Cencer, D, Vatne, M, Pulvermacher, K, Saenz, C, Kraemer, WJ, Robinson, B, Jones, P, Quebedeaux, N, Sprague, R, Dial, M, Carpenter, T, and Hagen, J. Relationship between objective measures of sleep and nocturnal cardiovascular physiology and swimming performance in collegiate female athletes: A Bayesian analysis. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-There is substantial evidence that sleep influences athletic performance; however, relationships with real-world competition outcomes remain unclear. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to explore the associations between objectively measured sleep, nocturnal cardiovascular physiology on the night before competition, and swim performance in female collegiate athletes. Female swimmers (n = 11) who wore a sleep monitoring device the night before competition, competed in the 200-yard freestyle (short course yard), and had ≥21 of 28 prior nights of valid data were included. Sleep metrics included total sleep time (TST), time in bed (TiB), and sleep efficiency (SE), whereas nocturnal cardiovascular metrics included heart rate variability (HRV) and resting heart rate (RHR) standardized as individualized z-scores. Race times were obtained from a publicly available database. Bayesian linear mixed-effects models estimated posterior probabilities of performance improvement. Results indicated a high probability that greater TST and TiB were associated with faster race times, with substantial support for improvements of at least 1 second per additional hour of sleep. In contrast, SE, HRV, and RHR showed low posterior evidence of meaningful associations with performance. These findings extend prior sleep and performance literature that has been confined to proxy assessments of athletic performance in controlled settings to real-world competition that should inform athlete education, emphasizing the importance of sufficient sleep opportunity and duration before competition.

title: Performance and Physiological Responses to Strength Training Programs in Elite Judo Athletes.
abstract: Campos, BT, Rodrigues, JGdS, Cal Abad, CC, Bachi, ALL, dos Santos, CMM, Tritto, AC, Kons, RL, Penna, EM, and Prado, LS. Performance and physiological responses to strength training programs in elite judo athletes. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study compared the effects of 2 short-term strength training models, block planning (BP) and undulating planning (UP), on performance, physiological, and perceptual responses in elite judo athletes. We hypothesized that BP would induce greater physiological strain due to the concentration of training stimuli. Eighteen judokas (14 men and 4 women) were randomly assigned to BP (n = 9) or UP (n = 9) for 4 weeks, performing 6 weekly strength sessions alongside technical-tactical training. Performance outcomes included countermovement jump (CMJ), muscle power (back squat and bent-over row), and the Special Judo Fitness Test (SJFT). Monitoring variables included internal load, heart rate variability (HRV), and well-being, while physiological markers included creatine kinase, tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), and cortisol. Data were analyzed using 2-way repeated-measures ANOVA (p < 0.05). Both groups improved SJFT performance (p < 0.01), with no between-group differences. Block planning increased lower-limb peak power (p = 0.01; d = 0.90), whereas UP showed no meaningful change. Upper-limb power and CMJ did not change in either group. Internal load showed different temporal patterns between models. Block planning presented higher HRVcv values (p = 0.04), indicating greater autonomic perturbation. Creatine kinase and TNF-α increased over time in both groups (p ≤ 0.05), while cortisol showed an interaction without clear post hoc differences. In conclusion, BP improved lower-limb power but increased physiological strain, whereas UP elicited similar judo-specific improvements with lower recovery demands. These findings highlight the importance of training organization for balancing performance and recovery in elite judo athletes.

title: Menstrual Cycle Phase-Dependent Lower Extremity Loading Patterns in Adolescent Female Athletes: Implications for Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury Risk.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Physically active females experience substantially higher anterior cruciate ligament injury rates than males, and postmenarche adolescent females commonly demonstrate high-risk mechanics. However, whether mechanics fluctuate across the menstrual cycle remains poorly understood in adolescent female athletes. The aim of this study was to examine differences in lower extremity kinematics and kinetics across two menstrual cycle phases (menstruation and mid-luteal) in postmenarchal adolescent female athletes during a dynamic change-of-direction task. It was hypothesized that biomechanical contributors to dynamic knee valgus would differ between phases.
METHODS: A controlled laboratory study was conducted. Thirty healthy postmenarchal adolescent female athletes (aged 13-17 years) were tested during menstruation (verified by self-reported active bleeding) and mid-luteal phase (scheduled via calendar-based day counting). Kinematics and kinetics were collected using 3-dimensional motion capture and force plates while participants performed a 45° run-cut task. Peak pelvis, hip, and knee angles and hip and knee moments were extracted during the loading phase for each limb. Linear mixed-effects models tested effects of phase and limb dominance (α = 0.05).
RESULTS: Participants were aged 15.6 ± 0.9 years, had a height of 168.8 ± 6.2 cm, and weighed 61.2 ± 7.0 kg, and a majority played soccer (70.0%). Compared with menstruation, the mid-luteal phase demonstrated greater peak anterior pelvic tilt (P = .018) and pelvic rise (P = .038), along with reduced peak knee flexion (P = .009). During menstruation, athletes exhibited greater hip abduction moment (P = .037), hip internal rotation moment (P = .043), knee valgus moment (P = .012), and knee external rotation moment (P = .007). Limb dominance effects were observed for pelvic rise (P < .001) and hip internal rotation moment (P = .047).
CONCLUSIONS: Biomechanical contributors linked to dynamic knee valgus differed by menstrual cycle phase in adolescent female athletes during a change-of-direction task. Menstruation was associated with greater coronal- and transverse-plane hip and knee loading, whereas mid-luteal phase was associated with reduced knee flexion and greater pelvic instability. Cycle-synced injury prevention strategies that are individualized and evidence-based may enhance lower extremity stability when knee control appears most challenged. However, while cycle-synced training may not be feasible in all settings, awareness of phase-related vulnerability may inform screening and load management.
KEY CONCEPTS: (1)Menstrual cycle phase may contribute to variability in lower extremity biomechanics during change-of-direction tasks in adolescent female athletes.(2)Biomechanical risk factors associated with dynamic knee valgus may differ between menstruation and mid-luteal phases.(3)Consideration of menstrual cycle phase may improve interpretation of biomechanical screening and performance testing.(4)Individualized injury prevention strategies may benefit from awareness of phase-related biomechanical changes.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: III.

title: Web-based rehabilitation after surgical salvage procedures for wrist osteoarthritis: protocol for a randomised controlled trial.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Wrist osteoarthritis (OA) is a disabling condition often affecting individuals of working age and frequently resulting from previous trauma. When non-operative management fails, surgical salvage procedures may reduce pain but require structured postoperative rehabilitation. Telerehabilitation has demonstrated comparable outcomes to standard face-to-face rehabilitation in several musculoskeletal conditions; however, evidence following its effectiveness after wrist OA surgery is lacking. This trial aims to evaluate whether a web-based rehabilitation programme is non-inferior to standard, face-to-face rehabilitation following surgical salvage procedures for wrist OA.
METHODS AND ANALYSIS: This is a prospective, parallel-group, assessor-blinded, randomised controlled non-inferiority trial conducted at a tertiary hand surgery centre. 90 adults undergoing surgical salvage procedures for wrist OA (four-corner fusion, lunocapitate fusion, scaphotrapeziotrapezoid fusion, radioscapholunate fusion or proximal row carpectomy) will be randomised 1:1 to receive either postoperative web-based rehabilitation or standard face-to-face rehabilitation. The primary outcome is the patient-rated wrist evaluation score measured 12 weeks after immobilisation has ended. Secondary outcomes include pain, health-related quality of life, fear of movement, range of motion, grip strength, patient-reported experience, adherence and cost of rehabilitation.
ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION: Ethical approval has been granted by the Swedish Ethical Review Authority in November 2024. Results will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications.
TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBER: NCT06814821

title: Effects of Whey Protein Supplementation on Muscle Damage, Hepatic Stress, and Inflammatory Markers in Power- and Endurance-Trained Athletes.
abstract: This study investigated the effects of 8 weeks of whey protein supplementation (30 g/day) on biomarkers of liver function, inflammation, and muscle damage in trained power-trained (predominantly speed-power/anaerobic-power disciplines) and endurance-trained athletes, in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled design. Fifty-nine male athletes were stratified into power (n = 30) and endurance (n = 29) groups, then randomly assigned to a whey protein group (WG) or a placebo control group (CG). Biomarkers assessed pre- and post-intervention included alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), C-reactive protein (CRP), and creatine kinase (CK). Significant reductions in ALT, AST, and CK were observed in both endurance- and power-trained athletes after supplementation (p = 0.001, p = 0.015, p = 0.001, and p = 0.003 respectively), indicating attenuated hepatic and muscular stress. Among the four biomarkers, only ALT displayed a statistically significant three-way interaction (Time × Supplementation × Training modality; p = 0.003), identifying it as the sole marker showing a genuine modality-specific differential response to supplementation. A significant within-group reduction in CRP was additionally observed in the supplemented power-trained athletes (p = 0.039), whereas endurance athletes showed only minor, non-significant changes; because the omnibus three-way interaction for CRP was not significant, this finding is reported as a within-group trend rather than evidence of a differential effect between modalities. Placebo groups demonstrated stable or increased enzyme and CRP values, particularly in endurance athletes. These findings suggest that whey protein may attenuate exercise-induced hepatic and muscular stress across training modalities, with a modality-specific effect on hepatic stress markers (ALT) observed in power-trained athletes. The results highlight whey protein's potential as a nutritional aid to promote recovery and physiological adaptation, possibly mediated by antioxidant and anti-inflammatory mechanisms. Further studies are warranted to examine long-term outcomes and dose-response effects across different training profiles.

title: Platelet Concentrates in Tooth Replantation: A Narrative Review and Evidence Synthesis of Periodontal and Pulpal Healing.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: The prognosis of an avulsed, replanted tooth over the long term hinges on whether the periodontal ligament (PDL) and the dental pulp can be preserved or regenerated. When extra-oral dry time is prolonged, PDL necrosis follows, and the root becomes prone to inflammatory or replacement (ankylotic) resorption. Platelet concentrates-platelet-rich plasma (PRP), leukocyte- and platelet-rich plasma (L-PRP), and platelet-rich fibrin (PRF)-are autologous biomaterials that supply growth factors and may influence this healing process. This review asks whether autologous platelet concentrates reduce inflammatory and replacement (ankylotic) root resorption and improve periodontal and pulpal healing after delayed or intentional tooth replantation, compared with no adjunct, and whether residual periodontal ligament (PDL) viability changes this effect.
MATERIAL AND METHODS: This narrative synthesis (not a systematic review) draws together recent controlled clinical and animal studies with the case-report and preclinical literature already captured in the only published systematic review on this topic. The search covered PubMed, Google Scholar, the Cochrane Library, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science, from January to May 2026.
RESULTS: In preclinical models, L-PRP and PRF promote pulpal repair, tertiary dentin formation, and attenuated inflammatory root resorption, although neither consistently prevents ankylosis once PDL viability has been lost. In one retrospective comparative study of intentional replantation in hopeless teeth, PRF combined with root-surface biomodification produced greater clinical attachment gain and a larger reduction in probing depth than replantation alone, a direction consistent with earlier case reports. Small, largely non-randomized samples and unstandardized protocols still limit this evidence.
CONCLUSIONS: Platelet concentrates are biologically plausible adjuncts that improve periodontal and pulpal healing indices, yet they do not reliably prevent ankylosis. Their clinical role will remain undefined until prospective randomized trials with standardized protocols are available.

title: Fueling the Modern Endurance Athlete: The High-Carbohydrate Revolution, Exogenous Ketones, and an Evidence-Based Approach for the Sports Medicine Clinician.
abstract:
CONTEXT: Carbohydrate is the principal limiting fuel for prolonged, high-intensity endurance exercise, and consensus guidelines have long capped recommended intake during exercise at approximately 90 g/h. Two developments have challenged and extended contemporary fueling practice: a shift toward carbohydrate intakes of 100 to 150 g/h in elite endurance sport, and widespread commercial availability of exogenous ketone supplements marketed as ergogenic aids. Both have outpaced the clinical evidence and have reached the competitive and recreational athletes who present to sports medicine clinicians.
EVIDENCE ACQUISITION: Narrative review of primary metabolic and performance studies, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and consensus statements published through mid-2026, identified through PubMed and reference tracing.
STUDY DESIGN: Narrative review.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 5.
RESULTS: Multiple-transportable-carbohydrate formulations (glucose plus fructose) raise exogenous carbohydrate oxidation above the roughly 1 g/minute ceiling imposed by intestinal glucose transport, providing the mechanistic basis for fueling rates of ≥90 g/h. Ingesting 120 g/h increases exogenous carbohydrate oxidation, but the best-controlled studies have not demonstrated additional endogenous (liver and muscle) glycogen sparing or a consistent performance advantage, and gastrointestinal tolerability requires deliberate gut training. For exogenous ketones, an influential 2016 study reported altered substrate use and improved time-trial performance. Subsequent trials and multiple systematic reviews and meta-analyses have not confirmed an acute ergogenic effect, and several have documented gastrointestinal distress or impaired performance. The more promising and reproducible signal for ketones lies in postexercise recovery and attenuation of overreaching. Finally, athletes who restrict in-competition and training carbohydrate to pursue leanness risk low energy and carbohydrate availability, the substrate of Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs).
CONCLUSION: Carbohydrate intake of ≤90 g/h, built through progressive gut training, is supported by consensus guidelines and mechanistic evidence for prolonged, high-intensity endurance events; progression toward 120 g/h is reasonable in selected, well-adapted athletes competing in the longest events, with the understanding that a performance benefit >90 g/h remains unproven. Routine exogenous ketone supplementation for acute performance is not supported by current evidence; a recovery-focused application is plausible and increasingly supported but requires further study. Clinicians should frame both strategies within adequate energy availability to protect long-term athlete health.Strength-of-Recommendation Taxonomy (SORT):B.

title: Dose-specific effects of caffeinated chewing gum on reactive blocking timing, jump mechanics, and neuromuscular responses after volleyball-specific fatigue in elite female volleyball players.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To investigate the effects of caffeinated chewing gum at nominal target doses of 3 and 6 mg/kg on reactive blocking timing, block-jump mechanics, and neuromuscular responses in elite female volleyball players under post-fatigue conditions.
METHODS: Fifteen elite female volleyball players completed a randomized, placebo-controlled crossover study implemented with double-blinding procedures. Participants consumed placebo (PLA), caffeinated chewing gum at nominal target doses of 3 mg/kg (CAF3) or 6 mg/kg (CAF6), and were tested after supplementation and warm-up at PRE and immediately after a volleyball-specific repeated blocking fatigue protocol (POST). Primary outcomes were reactive blocking timing-chain indices and block-jump (BJ) peak power. Secondary outcomes included additional BJ mechanical variables and general jump measures from countermovement jump (CMJ) and drop jump (DJ) tests. Exploratory outcomes included synchronized surface electromyography (sEMG) variables of lower-limb muscles. Participant blinding was assessed after each visit.
RESULTS: Fatigue impaired jump-related performance across conditions (p < 0.05). For the primary outcomes, the descriptive decline in BJ peak power was 6.9% in CAF6 versus 13.9% in PLA; the adjusted POST comparison did not establish superiority of CAF6 over CAF3. For timing outcomes, overall sequence time increased by 18.4% in PLA, 6.4% in CAF3, and 3.0% in CAF6; CAF6 therefore showed the smallest descriptive deterioration in the integrated sequence measure, whereas CAF3 showed little change in the mean stationary and movement component times. CAF6 showed a reduction in mean stationary response time and the smallest increase in overall sequence time. For secondary outcomes, caffeine showed more favorable post-fatigue responses in selected CMJ/DJ measures, including CMJ mean propulsive power and DJ contact time (p < 0.05), and CAF6 showed greater preservation of selected stretch-shortening cycle-related mechanical measures, including DJ jump height and DJ vertical stiffness, than PLA (p < 0.05). In contrast, CMJ mRSI showed a divergent pattern and was not interpreted as evidence of caffeine-related attenuation of fatigue-induced decrements. Exploratory sEMG results showed smaller post-fatigue changes in selected frequency-domain and activation-timing variables under CAF6, particularly in measures related to extensor-muscle function. Participant masking was incomplete: perceived caffeine ingestion was reported in 0.0%, 53.3%, and 80.0% of PLA, CAF3, and CAF6 visits, respectively, and adverse effects were more frequent in CAF6.
CONCLUSIONS: The observed responses were outcome-specific: CAF6 showed a smaller decline in BJ peak power and the smallest increase in overall sequence time, whereas CAF3 showed little change in mean stationary and movement response times. These findings do not establish a generally preferable dose or a timing-stability advantage for CAF3. Incomplete participant masking limits attribution of the differences exclusively to caffeine dose.

title: Low energy availability in recreational high-intensity functional training athletes: associations with health and performance outcomes.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Low energy availability (LEA) is the primary etiological factor underlying Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (RED-S), yet limited research has examined LEA risk and associated health and performance outcomes in recreational high-intensity functional training (HIFT) athletes. The purpose of this study was to evaluate energy availability (EA) and physiological outcomes aligned with the RED-S Health and Performance Models in a recreational HIFT cohort.
METHODS: Thirty participants (females: n = 18, males: n = 12; 31.2 ± 8.2 years) completed a two-week prospective observational study with repeated measures of energy intake, exercise energy expenditure, and associated health and performance-related measures. Energy intake was assessed via dietary logs, exercise energy expenditure was estimated using a wearable armband, and EA was calculated relative to dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry-derived fat-free mass. Participants were classified as LEA if EA was <30 kcal·kg-1 FFM·day-1. Performance-related outcomes included rating of perceived exertion (RPE), perceived recovery status (PRS), and total quality recovery (TQR). Health-related outcomes included sleep duration, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and bone mineral density (BMD) (reported by Z-Score).
RESULTS: Mean EA was 24.9 ± 9.7 kcal·kg-1 FFM·day-1, with 80% (n = 24) of participants demonstrating EA below the LEA classification threshold. The high prevalence of LEA should be interpreted cautiously given the potential for underreporting dietary intake. LEA status was not associated with differences in recovery, sleep quality, or BMD (p > 0.05), and EA was not significantly correlated with performance or health outcomes. In an exploratory analysis, sleep duration was moderately positively associated with TQR (ρ = 0.46, p = 0.01); however, this finding should be interpreted cautiously given the number of comparisons performed.
DISCUSSION: Despite the high prevalence of LEA, associated health and performance impairments were not detected, suggesting that measurable consequences of LEA may not be evident over a short observation period in recreational HIFT athletes. These findings support ongoing monitoring of EA, fueling practices, and recovery behaviors to reduce the potential long-term consequences associated with RED-S.

title: Associations between mental health conditions and outcomes of pain and function following upper extremity fragility fractures: A systematic review.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Upper extremity fragility fractures (UEFF) are increasingly prevalent among older adults and are associated with functional decline, recurrent fracture risk, and increased mortality. While physical comorbidities influence recovery, the impact of pre-existing mental health conditions on pain and function following UEFF is less clear.
PURPOSE: To synthesize evidence examining associations between pre-existing mental health conditions and pain and functional outcomes following UEFF.
STUDY DESIGN: Systematic review.
METHODS: A comprehensive search of MEDLINE, PubMed, PsycINFO, CINAHL, PEDro, SPORTDiscus, and the Cochrane Library was conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. Eligible studies included adults with UEFF that assessed mental health conditions (eg, depression, anxiety, and pain catastrophizing) identified prior to or within 2 weeks of fracture and reported pain or functional outcomes using validated measures. Risk of bias was evaluated using the Quality in Prognosis Studies (QUIPS) tool. Due to substantial heterogeneity in psychological constructs, outcome measures, and follow-up intervals, findings were synthesized narratively by short- (≤3 months), mid- (6-9 months), and long-term (≥12 months) follow-up.
RESULTS: Thirteen studies were included [10 distal radius fractures (DRF), three proximal humerus fractures (PHF)]. In DRF, short‑term outcomes were primarily associated with anxiety and pain catastrophizing, which predicted poorer grip strength, range of motion, and upper‑extremity functional performance. Mid‑term outcomes were influenced by psychological distress, pain interference, fear of movement, and self‑efficacy. At long‑term follow‑up, depression was the most consistent predictor of persistent disability, with affected individuals demonstrating worse functional scores and slower recovery trajectories. Antidepressant use and registry‑defined common mental disorders present before fracture were associated with poorer long‑term outcomes. In PHF, pre‑existing mental health diagnoses and kinesiophobia were associated with worse mid‑ to long‑term disability and quality‑of‑life outcomes.
CONCLUSIONS: Pre-existing mental health conditions are important prognostic factors for pain and functional recovery following UEFF. Incorporating early psychosocial screening and psychologically informed rehabilitation may improve outcomes.

title: Conceptual Frameworks and Assessment of Readiness to Train in Endurance Exercise: A Systematic Review.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Readiness to train has emerged as a construct to guide daily training prescription and recovery management in endurance athletes. However, its conceptual basis, assessment, and methodological quality and validity remain inconsistently defined. This systematic review aimed to (1) identify how readiness is defined in endurance exercise and (2) categorize tools used to assess it. As a secondary aim, the review evaluated the methodological approach of the studies employing these tools.
METHODS: Following PRISMA guidelines, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were explored. Eligible studies included endurance athletes aged 18-65 years, evaluating readiness before or after training or competition. Two reviewers independently screened, extracted data, and assessed quality using the revised Cochrane Risk of Bias tool. Fourteen studies were included.
RESULTS: Readiness definitions were inconsistent and frequently overlapped with related constructs such as recovery and fatigue. Ten studies used self-reported tools (fatigue, sleep, stress, and soreness). Nine studies assessed objective tools, including heart rate (HR) variability, resting HR, countermovement jump, and submaximal tests. HR variability-based approaches and individualized feedback were used to track autonomic recovery and guide training prescription, while on-field indices (eg, HR-running speed, HR-running power, countermovement jump) provided neuromuscular insights, although they can also be influenced by cardiovascular and metabolic factors. Overall, there was considerable heterogeneity in tools and their combinations, highlighting the lack of standardized approaches to assess readiness to train. Seven studies combined subjective and objective measures, suggesting a more comprehensive monitoring strategy. However, many of these tools were primarily used to assess related constructs (eg, fatigue, recovery, and training adaptation) rather than directly predict performance; consequently, their ability to predict performance outcomes remained limited or was not even assessed.
CONCLUSION: This review highlights substantial conceptual ambiguity, methodological limitations, and heterogeneity in readiness assessment. A multidimensional framework conceptualizing readiness as a dynamic psychophysiological state influenced by stress, recovery, and contextual factors may support more structured and meaningful monitoring in endurance athletes.

title: Effects of Morning Strength and Power Priming Exercises on Afternoon Physical and Cognitive Performance in Male Rugby Union Players.
abstract: The objective of this study was to assess the effect of morning strength and power priming exercises on afternoon physical and cognitive performance in male rugby union players. On two occasions in a randomised, counterbalanced design, 25 male rugby union players completed morning physical (countermovement jump, 40 m linear sprint) and cognitive (rapid visual information processing; spatial working memory; paired associates of learning) assessments. Control (passive rest) or intervention (barbell back squat, 3 × 3 repetitions at 85% of one repetition maximum and barbell squat jump, 5 × 3 repetitions at 40% one repetition maximum) trials were implemented 5.5 h before afternoon assessments. Differences between morning and afternoon assessments were found in sprinting performance following intervention for 30 m fly (-0.08 ± 0.13 s, p = 0.004, ES: 0.615) and 40 m (-0.12 ± 0.17 s, p = 0.001, ES: 0.711) relative to control (0.03 ± 0.07 s, p = 0.022, ES: -0.476; 0.01 ± 0.09 s, p = 0.740, ES: -0.065, 30 m fly and 40 m, respectively). Afternoon countermovement jump flight time improved following intervention compared with control (2% vs. 0%, p = 0.012, ES: -0.53). No changes were found for cognitive assessments (p > 0.05). Morning strength and power priming exercises combining heavy-load traditional and light-load ballistic exercises effectively enhanced vertical jump and sprint performance, but not cognitive performance, in the afternoon in male rugby union players.
