title: Genetic susceptibility to anterior cruciate ligament rupture in females: a systematic review of female-stratified candidate-gene evidence and the absence of genome-wide studies.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To systematically synthesise and critically appraise genetic association studies reporting female-stratified evidence for anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture.
DESIGN: Systematic review.
DATA SOURCES: Web of Science, Scopus, Ovid MEDLINE and the Cochrane Library were searched from database inception to 21 December 2025, which was the predefined search date for this review.
ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA FOR SELECTING STUDIES: Human genetic association studies reporting female-stratified ACL rupture outcomes or extractable female-only data were included. Studies reporting combined-sex analyses without extractable female data were excluded. Due to predefined heterogeneity in phenotypes, populations and genetic models, findings were synthesised narratively.
RESULTS: 19 studies met the inclusion criteria, predominantly small candidate-gene case-control designs. Importantly, these publications did not represent 19 independent cohorts. The largest prospective cohort included 790 women at risk at baseline, of whom 58 sustained an incident ACL injury and 732 remained without incident injury. COL5A1 rs12722 was the most frequently reported female-stratified candidate variant. Positive single-variant estimates principally concerned CC homozygotes under a recessive model and arose from South African samples with documented participant reuse. Separate allelic associations were also reported. Independence of this signal was limited by probable cohort overlap, heterogeneous genetic models and null prospective evidence. Evidence for other collagen, proteoglycan, inflammatory and extracellular matrix remodelling genes was inconsistent. No female-stratified genome-wide association studies were identified.
CONCLUSIONS: COL5A1 rs12722 is the most frequently reported female-stratified candidate variant, but independent replication is not established. Positive recessive estimates concern CC homozygotes and should not be extended to heterozygotes. Small samples, participant reuse, heterogeneous genetic models and null prospective evidence limit certainty. Female-stratified associations do not establish sex-specific effects. Evidence derives predominantly from women of European ancestry, and generalisability to other ancestries remains unknown. Current findings do not support genetic screening for ACL rupture risk in female athletes; adequately powered, female-stratified genomic studies with rigorous phenotyping and independent replication across diverse ancestries are needed.

title: Indications, Techniques, and Outcomes of Meniscus Centralization for Root Tears and Meniscus Transplantation: An International Expert Consensus Statement.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To develop an expert consensus statement on the biomechanics, diagnosis, surgical indications and techniques, rehabilitation protocols, and postoperative outcomes of centralization procedures in meniscus root pathology and meniscal allograft transplantation.
METHODS: A working group generated 39 statements on meniscal centralization from previously published data for evaluation in a 3-round modified Delphi process. A panel of 22 international experts rated each statement on a 5-point Likert scale, and statements were retained, revised, or excluded according to predefined thresholds (≥75% agreement and <20% disagreement). Rounds 1 and 2 included both literature-derived items and open-ended responses, allowing panel members to propose additional statements.
RESULTS: Ultimately, 35 statements were retained, with 100% participation across all rounds. The expert panel reached consensus that centralization may be considered in the setting of root repair and meniscal allograft transplantation to reduce meniscal extrusion (ME), improve joint contact mechanics, potentially enhance root healing, and limit displacement of the repair. The expert panel suggested that the degree of ME may help guide decision-making and that successful outcomes after medial meniscus posterior root repair with centralization may be evaluated by changes in ME and degenerative progression. Medial meniscus posterior root centralization should be considered when ME on magnetic resonance imaging exceeds 3 mm, and lateral centralization should be considered for lateral root tears with concomitant meniscofemoral ligament injury and >3 mm extrusion. Centralization was not recommended in advanced osteoarthritis. Panelists supported its use in symptomatic medial ME with varus deformity in combination with high tibial osteotomy. Transtibial tunnels, suture anchors, and hybrid constructs were all considered acceptable, provided that fixation is individualized to the location of ME and native meniscotibial anatomy and overtightening is avoided. The panel emphasized the need for long-term studies to confirm the durability and joint-protective benefits of centralization.
CONCLUSIONS: The panel supported consideration of meniscal centralization when magnetic resonance imaging shows extrusion greater than 3 mm in medial meniscus posterior root tears and in selected lateral root tears with concomitant meniscofemoral ligament injury and extrusion greater than 3 mm. Its use was discouraged in the setting of advanced osteoarthritis, whereas a combined approach with high tibial osteotomy was supported in patients with symptomatic varus-associated medial ME. No single fixation construct was preferred; transtibial, anchor-based, and hybrid techniques were all considered acceptable. Emphasis was placed on individualized surgical decision-making and on avoiding overconstraint.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level V, expert opinion.

title: Effects of Combined Blood Flow Restriction and Inter-Effort Recovery Hypoxia On Repeated-Sprint Performance And Physiological Responses: A Randomized And Single-Blinded Crossover Trial.
abstract: We investigated the acute effects of local and/or systemic hypoxia on performance and psycho-physiological responses during repeated cycle sprints. Eleven physically active young adults (six men, five women) performed four sessions on separate days, each involving three sets of five 5-s all-out efforts on a cycle ergometer (25 seconds rest between efforts and 5 minutes rest between sets). Sessions were conducted under four conditions, combining blood flow restriction [BFR; 45% of arterial occlusion pressure (AOP)] or control (CON; 5% of AOP) applied bilaterally to the legs during sprints, with inter-effort recovery hypoxia [IEH; inspired oxygen fraction (FiO2) = 13.5%] or normoxia (NOR; FiO2 = 20.9%). Power output decreased across sprints and heart rate increased over sets, with no differences between conditions (Δ = -9.18%). IEH resulted in lower peripheral oxygen saturation (Δ = -8.0%) but higher oxygen uptake (Δ = 6.7 mL·kg-1 min-1) and minute ventilation (Δ = 6.1 L·kg-1 min-1), compared to normoxic conditions. Blood lactate concentration increased (Δ = 6.5 mM) post-session similarly across all conditions. Vastus lateralis muscle oxygenation during sprints and inter-set recovery was comparable across conditions, although the mean tissue saturation index during inter-set recovery was lower in BFR + IEH versus CON + NOR conditions (Δ = -4.0%). Ratings of perceived exertion (Δ = 22.5%), limb discomfort (Δ = 34.2%), and breathing difficulty (Δ = 43.7%) increased throughout the sets, independently of conditions. Despite physiological and perceptual adjustments across sprint repetitions, neither BFR during sprints nor systemic hypoxia during recovery altered mechanical output in physically active individuals.

title: Upper-Extremity Tendinopathy and Enthesopathy in the Athlete: Best Evidence in Diagnostic and Therapeutic Advances.
abstract: Tendinopathy and enthesopathy represent common overuse conditions in athletic populations and frequently affect the upper extremity, particularly the rotator cuff, elbow extensor origin, and wrist extensors. These conditions arise predominantly from mechanical overload and are characterized clinically by load-dependent pain and impaired function. Following clinical evaluation, diagnostic evaluation frequently requires multimodality to exclude alternative pathology or inflammatory disease. Exercise-based rehabilitation remains the foundation of management, with contemporary evidence supporting progressive, individualized loading programs, including eccentric, concentric, isometric, and heavy slow resistance protocols, are tailored to symptom severity and sport-specific demands. Adjunctive modalities such as extracorporeal shock wave therapy demonstrate benefit in select chronic cases, particularly lateral epicondylitis and calcific shoulder tendinopathy. Although nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs and corticosteroid injections may provide short-term symptom relief, corticosteroids are associated with inferior long-term outcomes and potential deleterious effects on tendon structure. Biologic therapies, including platelet-rich plasma and topical glyceryl trinitrate, demonstrate heterogeneous results, and high-volume image-guided injections remain selectively used in refractory cases. Surgical intervention is reserved for patients with persistent symptoms following 6 to 12 months of comprehensive nonoperative care because most individuals achieve symptom resolution without operative management. Open, arthroscopic, and percutaneous techniques demonstrate comparable outcomes. Emerging technologies, including in-office nanoarthroscopy and bioinductive collagen scaffolds, show early promise but require further high-quality investigation.

title: Platelet-related extracellular vesicles: Therapeutic roles in musculoskeletal disorders.
abstract: Musculoskeletal disorders are a major cause of pain, disability, and loss of function. Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) has been widely investigated for musculoskeletal repair, and interest has increasingly extended to extracellular vesicle (EV) preparations obtained from platelet-related starting materials. These include EV-enriched preparations collected from isolated platelets or defined platelet concentrates (P-EVs), from PRP (PRP-EVs), and from platelet lysate (PL-EVs). They do not represent the same biological product. Their cellular contributors, co-isolated soluble components, and molecular composition can differ substantially, and the name of the starting material does not prove the origin of every vesicle in the preparation. Preclinical studies nevertheless suggest that these EV preparations can influence inflammatory responses, cartilage metabolism, tendon-cell behavior, and the local repair environment. The strength of this evidence varies with the source material, separation and characterization methods, experimental model, and delivery strategy. This review examines the therapeutic evidence for platelet-related EV preparations in musculoskeletal disorders, while keeping P-EVs, PRP-EVs, PL-EVs, and plasma-derived EVs distinct and considering the methodological limitations that currently restrict comparison and clinical translation.

title: Health, Risk and Adaptation in Extreme Open Water Swimming: A Qualitative Study of Channel Swimmers.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Participation in extreme open water swimming, including channel swimming, has increased markedly, yet health research has focused largely on quantifying risks rather than understanding athletes' lived experiences. This study explored how experienced channel swimmers perceive health issues, prevention strategies, and recovery across preparation, performance, and post-swim phases.
METHODS: A qualitative, interpretive study was conducted using semi-structured interviews with 30 swimmers who had completed at least two Oceans Seven channel swims. The study was conducted between April and September 2021. Interviews were transcribed verbatim and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Themes were developed inductively to capture physical, psychological, and management-related aspects of health.
RESULTS: Three interconnected themes were identified: (1) physical and physiological lived experience, (2) psychological and cognitive journey, and (3) proactive and reactive management. Pain, injury, and hypothermia were widely normalised as inherent to the sport, and chronic musculoskeletal problems were routinely managed rather than avoided. Notably, swimmers located maximum danger within the swim itself, while several of the most serious consequences-including swimming-induced pulmonary edema, pneumonia, and prolonged neurological symptoms-emerged only after completion. Psychological challenges included in-swim cognitive impairment, recognised only retrospectively, and post-swim emotional lows linked to the removal of a defining goal rather than to failure. Health management relied heavily on experiential knowledge, with swimmers using individualised strategies for preparation, real-time decision-making, and recovery. Recovery was viewed as an active, holistic process and a critical learning phase informing future swims.
CONCLUSIONS: Health in channel swimming is understood by athletes as a dynamic, adaptive process shaped by experience and community norms. These findings informed the development of TIDE (Training and Resilience, Intensity and Stress, Decision-making and Coping, Evolution and Feedback), a non-linear framework conceptualising marathon swimming as a continuous feedback loop in which each swim shapes preparation for the next. TIDE offers clinicians, coaches, and event organisers a framework for identifying, where an athlete's adaptive cycle is overwhelmed or temporarily disrupted, and provides a basis for formalising the experiential knowledge that currently protects only the most experienced swimmers as participation continues to grow.

title: Clinical validation of a vial wall-based dielectric barrier discharge plasma activation device for plasma-activated platelet-rich plasma preparation in osteoarthritis pain management.
abstract: Cold atmospheric plasma (CAP) has significant potential in biomedical applications. However, conventional plasma activation requires electrodes to contact a liquid directly, exposing it to the external environment. This conflicts with sterile, closed preparations required clinically. A vial wall-based dielectric barrier discharge (DBD) plasma activation device addresses this need by using standard clinical blood collection tube walls as a dielectric barrier. Electrodes contact only the tube exterior, never the liquid inside, and activation requires simply inserting the tube into the reactor chamber. Applied to platelet-rich plasma (PRP) therapy for osteoarthritis (OA), the device produced plasma-activated PRP (PA-PRP) with enhanced platelet activation, increased levels of transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β; 24%), platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF; 37%), and insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1; 32%), and broadly upregulated anti-inflammatory cytokines. In the destabilization of the medial meniscus (DMM) mouse OA model, PA-PRP treatment was associated with improved gait parameters and lower cartilage degeneration scores relative to PRP treatment. Human OA cartilage explants showed greater matrix staining after PA-PRP treatment. In an exploratory, randomized, single-blind split-body study involving three patients, PA-PRP-treated knees, compared with contralateral PRP-treated knees, showed numerically larger improvements in visual analog scale (VAS) pain score, Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) score, and effusion volume at week 15, with no adverse events during observation. These clinical observations are descriptive and hypothesis-generating, as the sample size precludes reliable efficacy or comparative safety inferences. Together, findings support device feasibility and PA-PRP use in OA and provide a rationale for adequately powered studies.

title: Increases in Agility and Quantitative Movement Quality Following a Coach-Led, Basketball-Specific Neuromuscular Training Warm-Up Programme in Adolescent Athletes.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Coach-led, basketball-specific neuromuscular training (NMT) warm-up programs have been shown to reduce injury risk. However, changes in agility and movement quality following such NMT in high school basketball players are not well characterized.
METHODS: In this pre-experimental study, high school basketball players (42 males, 31 females, 16 ± 1.4 years) performed a 10-minute, coach-led, basketball-specific NMT warm-up programme before practices and games (10-14 weeks). Changes in the Lane Agility Test (LAT) and single-leg squat (SLS) kinematics, encompassing trunk, pelvis, hip, and lower extremity kinematics and a composite score (SLS Score), from pre-to post-intervention were assessed. Relationships between pre-intervention scores, sex, the number of NMT sessions completed, and outcomes were assessed with linear regressions.
RESULTS: LAT completion times decreased following the NMT intervention, with larger changes associated with slower pre-intervention scores and more completed NMT sessions. SLS Scores were higher after the NMT intervention, potentially attributable to better pelvic and hip kinematics.
CONCLUSIONS: In this single-arm preliminary and exploratory study, favourable changes in agility and SLS kinematics following a coach-led, basketball-specific NMT programme were observed, with preliminary evidence of a dose-response relationship for agility. However, this study was non-randomized and lacked a control group. Therefore, these results should not be interpreted to suggest a causal relationship between the NMT performed and the changes in outcomes. In addition to NMT's role in injury prevention, coaches and players should be cognizant about performance and movement quality changes potentially associated with this accessible version of NMT.

title: Body recomposition in adults: mechanisms, modulators, and practical algorithms for simultaneous skeletal muscle mass gain and fat mass loss.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Body recomposition is the concurrent increase in fat-free mass (FFM) or skeletal muscle mass and decrease in fat mass (FM) within the same intervention period. Although hypertrophy is commonly pursued in energy surplus and FM loss in energy deficit, controlled trials indicate that recomposition can occur when progressive resistance training (PRT), adequate protein intake, and an appropriate energy prescription are combined.
METHODS: We conducted a structured narrative review of randomised trials, meta-analyses, and selected mechanistic studies in adults, with emphasis on FFM, FM, strength, and performance outcomes. Device heterogeneity was considered when interpreting evidence, with greatest weight placed on four-compartment and dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) outcomes.
RESULTS: PRT combined with higher protein intake, typically ~1.6-2.4 g/kg/day and higher relative intakes during energy restriction or leanness, is the most consistent strategy for recomposition. Effects are largest in untrained individuals and those with higher adiposity, smaller in trained or lean athletes, and still feasible in older adults when anabolic resistance is addressed with supervised PRT and sufficient protein. Moderate deficits, carbohydrate allocation around key sessions, sleep, and recovery support FFM retention or accretion while facilitating FM loss. Practical applications: Programmes should pair progressive overload with protein-centred diets, modest energy deficits, and periodic monitoring of body composition and performance.
CONCLUSIONS: Body recomposition is feasible but context-dependent; expected changes are generally modest in trained or lean populations and require individualised adjustment.

title: Is Better Diet Quality Linked to Better Competitive Functioning? An Integrative Multi-Analytic Study of Sleep Difficulty and Subjective Vitality Among Chinese Collegiate Athletes.
abstract: Background: Diet quality may be associated with recovery-related experiences and self-reported physical and psychological functioning in athletes. However, the roles of sleep difficulty and subjective vitality in these associations, together with their item-level network structure and predictive relevance, have not been examined within an integrated analytical framework. This study investigated the associations of diet quality with self-rated physical fitness and competitive psychological readiness among collegiate athletes and examined cross-sectional indirect associations involving sleep difficulty and subjective vitality. Methods: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 1641 collegiate athletes participating in provincial-level university sporting events in Yunnan and Guizhou, China. Assessments were completed on the athletes' competition check-in day. All core variables were assessed using self-report instruments, including diet quality, sleep difficulty, subjective vitality, self-rated physical fitness, and competitive psychological readiness, with the latter operationalized using mental toughness. Cross-sectional indirect associations were estimated using PROCESS Model 6. Regularized partial-correlation networks and bridge centrality analyses were used to characterize item-level conditional associations. Ridge regression and XGBoost were further applied to evaluate out-of-sample predictive performance, and SHAP values were used to quantify the relative predictive contribution of variables within the XGBoost models. Results: Higher diet quality was significantly associated with fewer sleep difficulties and with higher subjective vitality, self-rated physical fitness, and competitive psychological readiness. Significant indirect associations were observed involving sleep difficulty alone, subjective vitality alone, and the ordered sleep difficulty-subjective vitality term in both outcome models; the subjective-vitality-only estimate was the largest. Network analysis indicated that sleep-difficulty nodes were predominantly characterized by negative bridging connections, whereas subjective-vitality nodes showed primarily positive bridging connections across communities. In the predictive analyses, Ridge regression achieved holdout R2 values of 0.415 for self-rated physical fitness and 0.341 for competitive psychological readiness. In exploratory XGBoost analyses, subjective vitality showed the highest relative SHAP importance in both models. Conclusions: Diet quality was associated with self-rated physical fitness and competitive psychological readiness, operationalized using mental toughness, with additional indirect associations involving sleep difficulty and subjective vitality. These findings provide a conceptual basis for considering nutrition, sleep, and daytime vitality within an integrated athlete-support framework. Their temporal ordering and the effects of modifying these factors require longitudinal and experimental testing.

title: Vitamin D Insufficiency as a Nutritional Stress Amplifier: An Evidence-Weighted Framework for Adaptive Reserve under Exercise and Energy-Deficit Stress.
abstract: Vitamin D is a fat-soluble secosteroid whose biological activity depends on conversion of circulating 25-hydroxyvitamin D into calcitriol, the active ligand of the vitamin D receptor. Although vitamin D has often been discussed as a potential ergogenic nutrient, evidence for direct performance-enhancing effects in athletes remains inconsistent. This review proposes that vitamin D insufficiency, used here as a context-dependent descriptive label for low circulating 25(OH)D rather than as a universal diagnostic category, may function as a nutritional stress amplifier that narrows adaptive reserve when mechanical, energetic, endocrine, inflammatory, and neuroendocrine stressors converge. The strongest evidence derives from the vitamin D-calcium-phosphate-PTH-FGF23 axis, through which calcitriol-VDR signaling supports mineral homeostasis, skeletal remodeling, and resilience to repetitive skeletal loading. Emerging evidence suggests intersections with skeletal muscle repair, myokine and osteokine signaling, inflammatory regulation, and tissue adaptation, although athlete-specific validation is needed. Low energy availability and Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport provide a translational model in which low circulating 25(OH)D may become more relevant because multiple nutritional, endocrine, skeletal, and recovery stressors coexist. Brain-related pathways involving fatigue, sleep, HPA-axis-related recovery, BDNF, monoaminergic signaling, and interoceptive processing are retained only as hypothesis-generating domains, not as evidence that vitamin D status modifies cognition, mood, motivation, behavior, or central recovery mechanisms in athletes. Future studies should move beyond static 25-hydroxyvitamin D assessment and unstratified supplementation trials toward dynamic stress-recovery phenotyping. This framework positions low circulating 25(OH)D status as a testable conditional modifier of stress-recovery trajectories rather than an isolated determinant of athletic performance or a primary clinical target.

title: Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport and its Implications for the Foot and Ankle Surgeon.
abstract: Relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S) is a syndrome caused by low energy availability that affects multiple physiologic systems in both male and female athletes. Stress fractures of the foot and ankle are often the first signs of RED-S; therefore, it is crucial that orthopedic surgeons are aware of and able to identify this disorder. This article focuses on RED-S and provides a framework for understanding the disorder, it's relevancy to the orthopedic foot and ankle surgeon, and offers suggestions for diagnostic strategies and treatment approaches that are imperative for safe return to play.

title: Adolescent Sports-Related Lower Extremity Pain and Overuse Injuries.
abstract: Adolescent participation in organized sports has increased substantially in recent decades, accompanied by a rising incidence of lower extremity pain and overuse injuries. Unique physiologic characteristics of the growing athlete, including open physes and periods of rapid skeletal maturation, combined with early sport specialization and increasing training demands, place adolescents at elevated risk for overuse conditions. This review examines common causes of sports-related lower extremity pain in adolescent athletes, including patellofemoral pain syndrome, Osgood-Schlatter disease, patellar tendinopathy, Sinding-Larsen-Johansson disease, bone stress injuries, and symptomatic flexible flatfoot. For each condition, we review epidemiology, clinical presentation, diagnostic considerations, and contemporary management strategies. Most overuse injuries in this population are diagnosed clinically and respond well to conservative treatment that emphasizes activity modification, progressive rehabilitation, and load management. Imaging should be used judiciously, primarily to confirm diagnosis or exclude alternative pathology. Emerging therapies, including biologic injections and bone stimulation modalities, show promise in select conditions but require further high-quality evidence before routine adoption. Prevention remains central to reducing injury burden. Gradual progression of training load, neuromuscular conditioning, nutritional optimization, and monitoring during growth spurts are key strategies. Increasing evidence also suggests that psychosocial factors may influence injury risk. A multidisciplinary approach involving clinicians, coaches, and strength and conditioning professionals is essential to promote safe, sustainable sports participation and long-term musculoskeletal health in adolescent athletes.

title: Conductive Composite-Based Wearable Sensors for Sports Science: Intelligent Data Analysis and Emerging Applications.
abstract: Wearable sensors enable continuous acquisition of physiological, biochemical, and biomechanical signals during exercise, providing data to support sports performance assessment, training regulation, fatigue monitoring, and rehabilitation interventions. However, signal reliability and multidimensional data analysis under complex motion conditions remain constrained by device functionality. Conductive composites can improve sensor flexibility, interfacial conformability, and signal acquisition performance, while artificial intelligence (AI) enables movement pattern recognition, state assessment, and outcome prediction from complex data. Their integration is advancing wearable systems toward multimodal sensing and intelligent analysis. Guided by application needs in sports, this review summarizes emerging applications of wearable sensing technologies enabled by conductive composites and AI. First, the relevance to sports science and the data characteristics of physiological, biochemical, and biomechanical signals are introduced. The functional characteristics, representative applications, and major limitations of conductive polymer, carbon-based, MXene, and hydrogel composites are then summarized. Regarding algorithms, the fundamental principles of supervised learning, unsupervised learning, deep learning (DL), and large language models (LLMs) are discussed, with comparisons of their capabilities in feature extraction, temporal modeling, and multisource data analysis, as well as their input data requirements. On this basis, advances in the application of these systems to sports performance and sport-specific movement monitoring, exercise-induced fatigue monitoring and assessment, sports injury identification and evaluation, and intelligent monitoring of sports rehabilitation are reviewed followed by a discussion of current challenges and future directions. Through the coordinated integration of material design, signal acquisition, and intelligent analysis, wearable systems are expected to enable continuous, reliable, and individualized assessment of exercise-related states, with further applications in real-time feedback, risk alerts, and training decision support, providing a technological foundation for scientifically informed training, sports rehabilitation, and individual health management.

title: Sports-Related Back Pain and Injuries: From Muscle Strain to Spondylolisthesis.
abstract: Back pain is common in both the general population and young athletes, with risk increasing in sports that involve repetitive extension, rotation, and axial loading. Although most cases resolve with time, accurate diagnosis is essential to distinguish common musculoskeletal causes from more serious conditions. This article reviews key causes of athletic back pain, including muscle strain, mechanical low back pain, spondylolysis and spondylolisthesis, lumbar disc herniation, and sacroiliac joint dysfunction. It also examines diagnosis, treatment, and return to play considerations. Early recognition and appropriate management help ensure a safe and timely return to sport.

title: A narrative review on the translational and clinical application of platelet-rich plasma, bone marrow concentrate and microfragmented adipose tissue for meniscal tears.
abstract: Meniscal tears are a common knee pathology with an annual incidence of 66 per 100,000 patients and are associated with pain and an increased risk of osteoarthritis (OA). Orthobiological therapies have emerged as potential adjuncts to meniscal repair, but their clinical efficacy remains unclear. Minimally manipulated orthobiological therapies, including platelet-rich plasma (PRP), bone marrow aspirate concentrate (BMAC) and microfragmented adipose tissue (MFAT), have primarily been investigated in OA therapies, with their use as adjuncts for meniscal tears subsequently investigated. This review evaluates the preclinical and clinical evidence for PRP, BMAC and MFAT in the treatment of meniscal tears. A literature search was performed to identify preclinical and clinical studies investigating PRP, BMAC and MFAT for meniscal tears. Methodology with respect to therapeutic approach and tear type was noted, whilst outcomes relating to meniscal healing and patient-reported clinical outcome measures were evaluated from the selected evidence. PRP was the most extensively studied approach amongst the orthobiologics reviewed, with heterogeneous findings in both preclinical and clinical studies. In general, PRP did not demonstrate significant differences in clinical outcome scores (Visual Analogue Scale, International Knee Documentation Committee, Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score or Lysholm) compared with suture-only controls in clinical studies, although one clinical study reported a lower re-rupture rate with PRP (14.6%) compared to suture-only (17%). Selected preclinical studies of BMAC indicated greater meniscal healing compared with PRP, although comparative clinical evidence remains limited. Clinical evidence for MFAT treatment of meniscal tears was restricted to case studies for degenerative meniscal tears in OA patients, with selected studies demonstrating improvements in patient-reported outcomes from baseline, although no preclinical animal studies using this approach were found. Heterogeneity in the application of these orthobiologics, tear type treated and surgical approach has led to inconsistent findings within the selected studies. Current evidence does not demonstrate consistent clinical superiority of PRP, BMAC or MFAT over standard meniscal treatments. PRP has the broadest but heterogeneous evidence base, whereas comparative clinical evidence for BMAC and MFAT remains limited. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: N/A.

title: Understanding Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport.
abstract: Relative energy deficiency in sport (REDs) is a clinical condition resulting from low energy availability that affects physiological function and performance in athletes of all genders and ages. REDs is increasingly recognized in pediatric populations, particularly in endurance, aesthetic, and weight-class sports, such as long-distance running, gymnastics, and wrestling, respectively. REDs is a multisystem condition characterized by hormonal dysfunction, low bone density, or psychological disturbances, and is associated with increased injury risk and impaired performance. Management centers on restoring energy balance through nutritional and behavioral interventions, and prevention strategies emphasize education and early recognition. This review synthesizes current evidence on REDs in adolescent athletes, emphasizing current understanding of risk factors, clinical presentation, practical approaches to evaluation and management, and prevention strategies to support pediatricians in the management of REDs in the primary care setting.

title: Sports-related peripheral neuropathies in athletes: mechanisms, imaging evaluation, and sport-specific patterns.
abstract: Peripheral neuropathy in athletes is increasingly recognized as a significant source of morbidity, with injury patterns varying according to the biomechanical demands of specific sports. Although peripheral nerve disorders in athletes may result from acute trauma, they more commonly arise from chronic, repetitive mechanical stress inherent to athletic activity. Despite their frequency, they frequently remain underdiagnosed, as clinical manifestations often overlap with other musculoskeletal disorders. Mechanisms of injury include compression, traction, laceration, ischemia, and repetitive microtrauma. Distinct athletic modalities are associated with characteristic neuropathies reflecting sport-specific kinematics and loading patterns. Awareness of these biomechanical factors and recognition of typical clinical presentations are essential for accurate assessment of athletes with suspected nerve injury. Diagnostic evaluation frequently requires advanced imaging modalities, particularly magnetic resonance neurography (MRN) and high-resolution ultrasound (HRUS), which enable detailed structural assessment of peripheral nerves and detection of secondary imaging findings. Electrodiagnostic studies may provide complementary functional information in selected cases. Early and precise diagnosis is critical to guide management, facilitate safe return to sport, and prevent long-term functional deficits. While most nerve disorders respond to conservative treatment, severe, progressive, or refractory cases may warrant surgical intervention to restore function and enable return to play (RTP). This review examines mechanisms of injury, clinical evaluation, classification systems, imaging findings, and sport-specific patterns of peripheral nerve injury across diverse athletic disciplines.

title: Player, Coach, and Performance Staff Perceptions of, Experiences with, and Preferences for Nutrition Services Within Rugby: An Implementation‑Focused Qualitative Exploration.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: To explore how players, performance staff, and dietitians perceive, experience, and prefer nutrition services within professional rugby, a qualitative study using semi-structured interviews and thematic analysis, guided by an implementation science lens (Integrated Promoting Action on Research Implementation in Health Services, i-PARIHS), was conducted.
METHODS: Purposeful sampling was used to recruit 27 participants (13 professional players, 5 dietitians, 1 coach, 3 strength and conditioning coaches, 3 physiotherapists, 2 high-performance managers) from an Australian professional rugby organisation. Interviews were conducted online between April 2024 and July 2025, transcribed, inductively coded, and thematically analysed with iterative verification by multiple researchers. Analysis was completed to support understanding of factors that may influence implementation, including the i-PARIHS constructs of innovation, recipients, and context.
RESULTS: Three inter-related themes were generated. (1) Organisational value and role clarity determined dietitians' visibility, influence, and the credibility of nutrition messaging; when nutrition was not championed by leadership and performance staff, advice was fragmented and dietitians' contribution was reduced to narrow, "tangible" metrics. (2) Food practices were the primary vehicle through which nutrition services were enacted, including menu planning, food provision, shared meals, and food-literacy support; nutrition service gaps were most evident in women's, pathway, and rehabilitation contexts and for athletes experiencing food insecurity. (3) Limited resourcing constrained proactive delivery, relationship-building, and long-term planning, forcing reactive practice and uneven access across programs.
CONCLUSIONS: Nutrition was widely regarded as foundational to growth, preparation, recovery, broader training adaptation, and athlete well-being in rugby, yet current delivery models underperform due to undervaluation, blurred responsibilities, and insufficient staffing and food-system support. Findings suggest elevating dietetics to fully integrated, full-time roles and embedding equitable food-centred provision and food-literacy interventions are necessary to improve consistency, uptake, and athlete outcomes, and to reduce avoidable inequities between squads nationally.

title: Prebiotics in sport and exercise: current evidence, practical applications, and methodological considerations.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Prebiotics are selectively utilized by the host microbiota and can confer health and/or performance benefits, in part through increasing the abundance of beneficial gut microorganisms and their metabolites. While several studies have shown promising initial findings, high-quality scientific evidence examining the effects of prebiotics on athlete performance, health and wellbeing remains limited.
METHODS: This narrative review summarizes the current available evidence on prebiotic intake in athletic populations, including effects on gastrointestinal structure and function, immune responses, recovery, sleep, wellness, mood and exercise performance. In areas where there is limited evidence in athletic cohorts, but a physiological rationale for a benefit, findings from sedentary and/or clinical populations are evaluated, and the potential relevance of these findings to athletes are discussed. Finally, considerations for practitioners around the use of prebiotics with athletes are provided, and recommendations for designing future prebiotic-based research are explored.
RESULTS: Despite the limited existing literature around prebiotic use in athletes, there are several studies that indicate their potential to improve gut barrier integrity and reduce the incidence/severity of gastrointestinal symptoms. Data also indicates that prebiotics can increase salivary Immunoglobulin A secretion rate and reduce the duration and/or severity of upper respiratory symptoms in trained individuals. Other areas with emerging evidence that warrant further investigation in athletic populations include prebiotics' ability to support exercise adaptation and recovery, promote sleep improvements and enhance mood and cognitive function. The interpretation of current studies is limited by the lack of gut microbiome and metabolome measures and the absence of robust performance measures following a period of prebiotic supplementation. Well-controlled, adequately powered studies incorporating these outcomes are needed to determine the contexts in which prebiotic intake can meaningfully improve health and performance metrics, and to elucidate the underlying physiological mechanisms of any beneficial effects.
CONCLUSION: Prebiotic intake represents a promising intervention to attenuate exercise-induced disturbances to the intestinal epithelium, reduce exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms, and lower the duration/severity of upper respiratory symptoms in athletes. Future studies should prioritize high-quality performance assessments, alongside comprehensive microbiome and metabolome profiling, to elucidate mechanistic effects. Areas with limited current evidence such as recovery, sleep, mood, cognitive function, bone health and nutrient absorption in athlete cohorts should also be further explored.

title: Lateral meniscus posterior root tears in the anterior cruciate ligament-injured knee: Current concepts.
abstract: Lateral meniscus posterior root tears (LMPRTs) compromise load transmission and secondary stability in the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL)-injured knee and may be missed on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). This narrative current-concepts review addresses incidence, risk factors, biomechanics, diagnosis, classification, treatment, and outcomes, while distinguishing root tears from lateral meniscal oblique radial tears (LMORTs). Primary ACL reconstruction (ACLR) cohorts report LMPRT frequencies of 7.1%, 10.0%, and 12.2%; a mixed primary/revision cohort reports 6.6% and selected revision cohorts report 20.5% and 40.7%. These study-specific estimates differ in lesion definition and ascertainment. Contact injury, concomitant medial meniscal pathology, and increased lateral posterior tibial slope are recurring associations. Individual MRI signs have limited sensitivity; combined assessment and arthroscopic inspection and probing support diagnosis. LaPrade et al. describe root-tear morphology, Forkel and Petersen additionally consider meniscofemoral ligament integrity, and LMORT typing describes posterior-horn oblique radial tears. The systems overlap for near-root lesions and are descriptive frameworks rather than validated treatment algorithms. Selected stable lesions may be observed; repairable unstable lesions are generally treated with footprint fixation or side-to-side repair, according to anatomy and tissue quality. Repair with ACLRn is associated with improved patient-reported outcomes and high complete-or-partial healing proportions in selected series. Clinical improvement in ACL graft survivorship has not been demonstrated. Heterogeneous definitions, predominantly lower-level evidence, variable rehabilitation, and limited long-term comparative data, constrain conclusions about cartilage preservation and optimal treatment.

title: A mechanically active microneedle platform integrated with engineered exosomes for enhanced tendon-bone regeneration.
abstract: Functional regeneration of the tendon-bone interface remains a major challenge because early healing is constrained by an adverse inflammatory microenvironment and insufficient mechanical cues. Here, we developed a mechano-regenerative strategy that combines YAP-primed engineered exosomes with localized biomaterial-based delivery and active mechanical stimulation. Exosomes derived from a YAP agonist (PY-60) preconditioned TDSCs (P-Exo) showed enhanced uptake and promoted the osteogenic and chondrogenic differentiation of bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells, accompanied by activation of YAP-associated signaling and PI3K-Akt-related pathways. To improve local retention, P-Exo were incorporated into a ROS-responsive adhesive hydrogel, which accelerated fibrocartilage formation, bone ingrowth, and biomechanical restoration in a rabbit tendon-bone healing model. To address more complex repair conditions, we engineered a three-layer self-contracting microneedle platform for deep-tissue delivery of P-Exo with concurrent active mechanical stimulation. In an infected rat rotator cuff model, this system reduced bacterial burden and oxidative stress, promoted a reparative macrophage polarization and angiogenesis, and improved tendon-bone structural regeneration, biomechanical strength, and functional recovery. Together, these findings support a therapeutic framework in which engineered exosome signaling and active mechanoregulation act in concert to enhance tendon-bone repair.

title: How Effectively Does Protective Sports Gear Prevent Sports Injuries?
abstract: As organized and recreational sports continue to grow in popularity, associated sports injuries increasingly burden athletes. Protective sports gear is intended to reduce injury risk during play. This article provides a comprehensive review of the mechanism and efficacy of protective sports gear in injury prevention to the head and neck, upper extremity, and lower extremity and assesses where perhaps evidence for protection is lacking. Helmets, face shields, and protective eyewear have clear benefits in structural protection against injury. The impact of sports gear in reducing sport-related concussion is more variable, largely due to the repetitive nature of the injury mechanism where cumulative low-magnitude impacts contribute to brain injury. For the upper extremity, wrist guards have a clear benefit in reducing major and minor injuries among gymnasts and snowboarders and hence by inference on other impact sports. Ankle braces and taping potentially reduce the risk of ankle sprains among athletes, and the mandating of shin guards in professional soccer results in decreased sports-related lower extremity fractures. Further research is warranted to evaluate the effectiveness of sports gear on reinjury prevention and to study the implications of sports gear on risk compensation theory in athletes.

title: Comparison of Achilles tendon loading between rocker-soled and advanced footwear technology shoes during running in healthy individuals.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Achilles tendinopathy is a common running-related injury, and footwear characteristics may influence Achilles tendon loading. This study investigated the effects of rocker shoes and advanced footwear technology (AFT) shoes on Achilles tendon (AT) force during running.
METHODS: Nineteen healthy adult males with normal foot posture performed rearfoot strike running at a controlled speed under three footwear conditions: neutral, rocker, and AFT shoes. Peak AT force, AT force impulse per step, ankle joint angle, anterior ground reaction force, and stance time were compared among the three conditions.
RESULTS: No significant differences in ankle joint angle or stance time were observed among the footwear conditions. Compared with neutral and AFT shoes, rocker shoes significantly reduced peak AT force, AT force impulse per step, and peak anterior ground reaction force. No significant differences were observed between AFT and neutral shoes for any AT force-related variable.
CONCLUSIONS: Rocker shoes reduced Achilles tendon loading during running, whereas AFT shoes did not significantly alter Achilles tendon loading compared with neutral shoes. The reduction in tendon loading was accompanied by a lower peak anterior ground reaction force, which may reflect reduced propulsive demand at the ankle joint. Rocker shoes may therefore be beneficial for reducing mechanical loading of the Achilles tendon during running.

title: Foot and Ankle Sports Injuries: Diagnosis, Treatment, and Contemporary Orthopedic Innovations for the General Practitioner.
abstract: General practitioners (GPs) are frequently the first clinicians to evaluate athletic and nonathletic foot and ankle injuries. Six common foot and ankle conditions seen by GPs are Achilles tendon injuries, lateral ankle ligament sprains, plantar plate injuries/turf toe, ankle fractures and syndesmotic injuries, Lisfranc injuries, and fifth metatarsal base fractures. For each condition, this review outlines clinical diagnostic features, appropriate use of imaging, and decision making regarding conservative management strategies versus surgery. Nonoperative management initiated by GPs include functional bracing, protected weight bearing, activity modification, and structured rehabilitation protocols. Indications for orthopedic referral, such as failure of conservative management, mechanical instability or joint laxity on examination, radiographic evidence of displacement or unstable fracture, high-grade ligamentous or plantar plate disruption, and involvement of high-demand athletes, also are reviewed. By understanding common patient presentations, appropriate initial management, and indications for referral to orthopedic specialists, GPs can optimize early care, reduce diagnostic delay, and improve long-term functional outcomes for patients with foot and ankle sports injuries.

title: Understanding the Complexity of Athlete Sleep: A Systems Approach to Modelling the Athlete Sleep Environment.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Athlete sleep can be disrupted by sport- and non-sport-related factors. However, the interactions of these sleep-related factors are not well understood. Systems science approaches, such as causal loop diagramming (CLD), provide an opportunity to map these interactions. This project aimed to (1) develop a CLD of the athlete sleep system describing the interacting variables, (2) identify feedback loops and potential leverage points to optimise athlete sleep, and (3) demonstrate the applicability of a CLD to guide the development of a sleep monitoring framework.
METHODS: A systems-based model of athlete sleep was developed using CLD, informed by existing literature and refined through a consensus process involving ten subject matter experts (nine from Australia, one from the USA). The model was then interrogated using network analysis to identify key variables based on their position and connectivity within the system. These findings informed the development of a generic sleep monitoring framework.
RESULTS: The CLD comprised 48 variables and 120 relationships across four domains: travel demands, behavioural and lifestyle factors, athlete condition and readiness, and resourcing and scheduling constraints. Overall, 12 key variables were identified, with hours of travel, number of time zones crossed, dose of caffeine, and amount of resources or expenditure available being the most connected upstream variables. Level of pre-sleep arousal, sleep opportunity, travel fatigue, and level of performance received the greatest number of incoming relationships, representing points at which multiple pathways converge. Physical condition, level of performance, quality of diet, and importance of competition most frequently linked different quadrants of the system. These variables informed a three-tier monitoring framework capturing upstream determinants and downstream consequences of sleep.
CONCLUSIONS: According to the CLD, sleep health in athletes extends beyond an individual behaviour issue and is influenced by the structure and functioning of sport systems. Interactions among travel demands, physical readiness, behavioural and lifestyle factors, and organisational constraints sustain athlete sleep health over time. Consequently, meaningful improvements in sleep health are likely to arise from both system-level interventions and individual behaviour change strategies.

title: Treatment of clavicle fractures in adolescents.
abstract: Clavicle fractures constitute 10% to 15% of all fractures in adolescents. Historically, adolescent clavicle fractures have been treated non-operatively. Although recent data in the adult population has led to an increased rate of operative fixation in the adolescent population, a vast majority of these fractures in adolescents can be managed conservatively. This manuscript provides an overview of the current standard of care for clavicular fractures in adolescents in the context of sports medicine practices. To achieve this, a nonsystematic search of computerized databases of peer-reviewed articles was conducted, and a critical appraisal of existing literature was subsequently performed. Middle third clavicle fractures are by far the most common type and a vast majority of these fractures can be treated non-operatively with a sling given the robust healing and remodeling seen in adolescents. Lateral third fractures are far less common but may pose a risk for nonunion according to adult literature. Medial third fractures are the least common type and while they are typically non-displaced, patients with posteriorly displaced medial third fractures must have concomitant intrathoracic injury ruled out. Additionally, timing of the injury relative to competitive season could play a role in decision making as surgical fixation of clavicle fractures has been shown to yield faster return to play times.

title: Temporal coupling shapes the effects of prolonged muscle-tendon vibration on sensorimotor EEG activity during motor imagery.
abstract: Motor imagery (MI) recruits sensorimotor networks overlapping those engaged during physical execution and represents a promising rehabilitation tool. While concurrent afferent stimulation enhances MI-related cortical engagement, the effects of prolonged proprioceptive conditioning prior to MI remain unexplored. This study investigated whether prolonged muscle-tendon vibration (MTV) could modulate cortical activity during subsequent MI, indexed by electroencephalographic alpha- and beta-band event-related desynchronization (ERD). Twenty healthy adults performed imagined maximal isometric knee extensions before and after 20-minute suprapatellar MTV (100 Hz) or SHAM vibration (30 Hz with foam interface) in counterbalanced sessions. Cortical engagement was assessed via EEG burst detection over central electrodes (C3, Cz, C4). Maximal force capacity, submaximal force estimation performance, and cortical responses during combined MI and MTV were also evaluated. MTV induced stronger vibratory responses than SHAM, consistent with enhanced proprioceptive afferent activation. Following MTV, voluntary force outcomes showed near-threshold changes consistent with the expected direction, namely reduced maximal force capacity and altered submaximal force calibration, suggesting modified proprioceptive feedback. MI performed after MTV conditioning exhibited reduced alpha- and beta-band ERD compared to SHAM, with greater vibratory-induced responses being associated with a less pronounced post-vibration beta ERD. Conversely, when MI was performed concurrently with MTV following conditioning, alpha-band ERD increased selectively in the MTV session, with no modulation in the beta band. These findings suggest that prolonged proprioceptive conditioning modulates MI-related cortical engagement differently depending on the sensorimotor context in which imagery is performed. Such state-dependent effects may support distinct intervention strategies aimed either at recalibrating maladaptive sensorimotor patterns or at enhancing cortical recruitment in rehabilitation contexts.

title: Creatine and Beta-Alanine Supplementation for Endurance Athletes: Ergogenic Aids for Reaching the Podium?
abstract: Endurance sports are characterized mainly by prolonged exercise demands. Although endurance performance is primarily supported by aerobic metabolism, anaerobic energy pathways, buffering capacity, neuromuscular resilience, and the ability to tolerate fatigue during decisive moments of a race are also relevant to competitive success. In this context, creatine and beta-alanine supplementation are two ergogenic strategies purported to enhance endurance performance. This review critically examines the physiological rationale and current evidence regarding creatine supplementation, beta-alanine supplementation, and their cosupplementation in endurance sports. The available literature suggests that beta-alanine may improve performance in exercise tasks performed in the aerobic-anaerobic transition zone, through increased skeletal muscle carnosine content and enhanced intracellular buffering capacity. Creatine supplementation may support endurance performance by increasing phosphocreatine availability, improving glycogen resynthesis and buffering capacity, attenuating exercise-induced inflammation and muscle damage, preserving fast-twitch muscle characteristics, and enhancing repeated sprint ability or late-race power output. However, evidence supporting improvements in classical markers of aerobic performance, such as VO2max, lactate threshold, and time-to-exhaustion, remains inconsistent, and the available evidence has been derived from untrained or recreationally active individuals, limiting direct translation to highly trained endurance athletes. Therefore, the practical relevance of these supplements appears to depend on the athlete's training phase, event characteristics (e.g., weight-bearing or not), competitive goal, and performance level. Creatine and beta-alanine should not be viewed as universal ergogenic aids for endurance athletes, but rather as targeted nutritional strategies that may be particularly useful in race contexts where repeated high-intensity efforts, fatigue resistance, and decisive finishing actions influence performance.

title: Dysphagia as the Initial Manifestation of Anti-HMGCR Antibody-Positive Immune-Mediated Necrotizing Myopathy Complicated by Pulmonary Embolism.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anti-3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A reductase (anti-HMGCR) antibody-positive immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM) is a rare autoimmune myopathy characterized by progressive proximal muscle weakness and markedly elevated creatine kinase levels. Although commonly associated with prior statin exposure, statin-naïve cases and atypical presentations are well described. Patients with idiopathic inflammatory myopathies are also at increased risk for venous thromboembolism (VTE), though data specific to IMNM remain limited.
CASE PRESENTATION: An 83-year-old man with brief, remote statin exposure presented with progressive proximal muscle weakness and a three-year history of oropharyngeal dysphagia preceding limb involvement. Laboratory evaluation revealed markedly elevated creatine kinase and transaminases. Anti-HMGCR antibodies were positive, and muscle biopsy confirmed necrotizing myopathy. During evaluation for occult malignancy, bilateral pulmonary emboli were incidentally identified. The patient required high-dose corticosteroids, mycophenolate mofetil, and intravenous immunoglobulin for refractory disease. With aggressive immunosuppressive therapy and rehabilitation, he demonstrated substantial clinical recovery at 6 months.
CONCLUSION: This case highlights oropharyngeal dysphagia as an early and, for a prolonged period, isolated manifestation of anti-HMGCR antibody-positive IMNM; here, it preceded the onset of limb weakness by approximately 3 years. It underscores the importance of comprehensive diagnostic evaluation in patients with unexplained oropharyngeal dysfunction, in whom an inflammatory myopathy may otherwise be overlooked for years. Clinicians should maintain awareness of thrombotic risk in inflammatory myopathies, particularly during active disease. Early recognition and prompt immunosuppressive therapy remain critical to optimize outcomes and prevent irreversible muscle damage.

title: 18-years Follow-up after Mosaicplasty in Adolescent Athletes with Osteochondritis Dissecans of the Elbow.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Autologous osteochondral mosaicplasty is an established surgical treatment of unstable osteochondritis dissecans (OCD) lesions of the elbow. However, the information on the long-term outcomes is lacking. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the long-term clinical and radiographic results after autologous osteochondral mosaicplasty in the treatment of OCD of the elbow.
METHODS: This prospective long-term follow-up study is an extension of previously published data on 10 patients treated with autologous osteochondral mosaicplasty due to advanced, unstable OCD at the capitellum from 2003-2007. Objective and patient-reported outcomes were evaluated including Mayo Elbow Performance Score (MEPS), Oxford Elbow Score, Quick-Disability of the Arm, Shoulder, and Hand (Quick-DASH), Timmerman-Andrews Score, a Subjective Elbow Value, and Range of Motion (ROM). Radiographic signs of osteoarthritis were graded according to the Kellgren-Lawrence classification.
RESULTS: At mean 18 years (range 16.0-19.7) five patients were available for follow-up. Mean age at follow-up was 34.4, and all five patients were women. MEPS was a median 100 (range 85-100). Activities of daily life were mildly affected in two patients. Two patients had non-symptomatic osteoarthritis grade 1 and 2. Patients experienced a functioning and near-normal elbow.
CONCLUSION: The long-term results after mosaicplasty are encouraging, and we find it reasonable to recommend mosaicplasty as the surgical treatment in this group of female patients with advanced, unstable OCD lesions of the elbow. However, it is of concern that two out of five patients had non-symptomatic early radiographic signs of osteoarthritis at an early age. As this study has an inclusion rate of 50 % of the original cohort, attrition bias must be taken into consideration.
LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV, case series, treatment study.

title: High-Strength Tape for Cable Structure Reconstruction During Arthroscopic Repair of L-Shaped Rotator Cuff Tears.
abstract: With the innovation and progressive maturation of arthroscopic techniques, the advantages of minimally invasive surgery and accelerated rehabilitation have made arthroscopy a preferred option for patients with rotator cuff injuries. However, for complex rotator cuff tears, such as "L-shaped" tendon tears, the risk of postoperative retear remains considerable. The cable structure, serving as a "suspension bridge" within the rotator cuff, is a critical load-bearing component of the shoulder joint. This structure is frequently compromised in "L-shaped" rotator cuff tears. In this report, we describe an arthroscopic technique using high-strength tape to restore the cable structure and treat "L-shaped" rotator cuff tears. The key steps include using high-strength tape to reduce the retracted tendon stump and restore the cable structure, thereby re-establishing mechanical integrity, reducing tension on the repaired tendon, and minimizing the cutting effect of sutures on the tendon. Finally, the sutures from the medial-row anchor are employed to perform a "Margin Convergence" repair of the longitudinal tear component.

title: Therapeutic potential of umbilical cord-derived MSCs in arthritis: Insights from preclinical and clinical studies.
abstract: Among different types of arthritis, osteoarthritis (OA) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) remain the most common and primary cause of pain and disability worldwide, characterized by progressive joint degeneration and persistent inflammation. Although there have been developments in pharmacology, the available treatment program slows disease progression and provides only symptomatic relief. However, their ability to repair and restore damaged tissue is limited. This highlights the importance of regenerative therapy in actively modulating the immune system while stimulating tissue regeneration. We conducted a narrative review of PubMed, Scopus, Web of science, ClinicalTrials.gov, and ChiCTR, focusing on preclinical and clinical studies of umbilical cord-derived mesenchymal stem cells (UC-MSCs) therapy in OA and RA. Recently, UC-MSC have been emerging as a promising therapeutic approach due to their immunomodulatory and regenerative properties. Because they are harvested noninvasively, these cells have greater proliferative capacity and lower immunogenicity than MSCs derived from bone marrow or adipose tissue. UC-MSCs do not replace damaged cells; instead, they signal other cells to produce bioactive substances that reduce inflammation and promote cartilage repair. Data from emerging preclinical and clinical trials, which show significant improvements in WOMAC and VAS scores and a decrease in DAS28 with minimal adverse effects, suggest that UC-MSCs will improve pain and function and, in turn, overall quality of life. UC-MSCs represent a mechanistically distinct and clinically promising therapeutic effect for OA and RA, addressing both the inflammatory and degenerative condition of joint disease. However, there are still large, well-designed, standardized clinical trials that can best optimize doses and treatment plans. This narrative review summarizes the various forms of arthritis, disease pathogenesis, and preclinical and clinical evidence for the use of UC-MSCs in the treatment of arthritis, such as OA and RA.

title: Relationship between lower extremity isokinetic strength ratio and dynamic balance ability in elite combat sports athletes.
abstract: Dynamic balance is essential for performance and injury prevention in combat sports, but its relationship with isokinetic strength ratios of the lower extremity and trunk is not well understood. This study investigated the associations between knee, hip, and trunk strength ratios and dynamic balance in elite combat sport athletes. Fifty-one elite judo and wushu athletes (31 males, 20 females) underwent isokinetic testing of the knee, hip, and trunk, with peak torque normalized to body mass (%body weight). Dynamic balance was assessed using the Biodex Balance System SD. Interaction effects between strength ratios and balance variables were analyzed using three-way analysis of variance. Male athletes showed greater muscle strength, whereas female athletes demonstrated better dynamic balance. Higher knee flexor-to-extensor strength ratios (≥61%) and moderate hip (35%-40%) and trunk strength ratios were associated with better dynamic balance. Significant interaction effects were found between knee and hip strength ratios. Our findings suggest that dynamic balance in elite combat sport athletes may depend on the coordinated strength balance of the knee, hip, and trunk rather than on absolute muscle strength alone.

title: Shoulder Evaluation and Management in the Athlete: From Examination to Surgical Indications.
abstract: Shoulder injuries are common among athletes and encompass a wide spectrum of pathology resulting from contact, overhead motion, and repetitive loading. Evaluation of the athletic shoulder presents unique challenges because symptoms may be subtle, sport specific, and performance limiting rather than overtly painful. Accurate diagnosis requires a systematic approach that integrates a detailed history, focused physical examination, and appropriate use of imaging and diagnostic adjuncts. This article provides a clinically oriented review of shoulder evaluation and management in athletes, emphasizing common athletic shoulder pathologies, including rotator cuff disease, instability, labral injury, and overuse conditions. Principles of nonoperative management are discussed along with indications for surgical referral based on structural injury, failure of conservative treatment, and sport-specific demands. Our objective is to equip clinicians with a practical framework to guide diagnosis, management, and return-to-play decision making across a broad range of athletic contexts.

title: Post-Exercise Thermal Interventions and Nocturnal Sleep in Athletes: A Narrative Review of the Potential Underlying Physiological Mechanisms.
abstract: Sleep is essential for optimal performance and recovery in athletes. Post-exercise cold exposure, including cold water immersion and cryotherapy, is typically used to enhance recovery, but its effects on sleep remain unclear. Emerging evidence also suggests that post-exercise heat exposure, including sauna and hot water immersion before sleep may improve both objective and subjective sleep outcomes. However, the effectiveness of post-exercise thermal interventions for improving nocturnal sleep in athletes specifically has not yet been comprehensively evaluated. This narrative review synthesizes the current evidence and discusses the potential physiological mechanisms by which post-exercise thermal interventions may influence nocturnal sleep in athletes. Despite methodological heterogeneity, existing research indicates that post-exercise thermal interventions may influence the subsequent nocturnal sleep of athletes through multiple and varying interacting mechanisms. For example, cold exposure close to bedtime (< 2 h) may disrupt sleep by reducing the distal-to-proximal skin temperature gradient (DPG), thereby increasing sleep onset latency and shortening sleep duration. In contrast, when applied more than 2 h before bedtime, cold exposure may improve sleep by augmenting parasympathetic tone and/or reducing muscle soreness and associated nocturnal movement. Although it remains unclear whether post-exercise heat exposure improves sleep via autonomic modulation or reduced muscle soreness, existing evidence indicates that sleep may be facilitated by an increased DPG. Moderating factors such as sex, time of day, environmental temperature, bedding microclimate, acclimatization status, and training load may influence the effects of post-exercise thermal interventions on sleep and should be investigated in future studies.

title: Spatial transcriptomics in immune-mediated necrotising myopathy uncovers a specific necrotic signature related to immune-driven fibrosis.
abstract: Immune-mediated necrotising myopathies (IMNM) are characterised by muscle fibre necrosis, complement deposits around non-necrotic fibres, and macrophage infiltrates. Patients experience muscle damage with fibro-fatty replacement, leading to poor strength recovery, but the pathogenesis remains unclear. To investigate IMNM pathogenesis, we applied spatial transcriptomics on myositis muscle biopsies and integrated the results with published single-nucleus transcriptomic data. This combined approach enabled analysis of gene expression with spatial localisation in the muscle. Inflammatory, fibrotic, regenerative, and lipid metabolism-related signatures were identified in IMNM, distinct from other myositis, with specific distribution in necrotic and peri-necrotic regions. A unique subtype of immune-driven fibroblasts expressing SFRP4 was enriched in IMNM necrotic areas. These cells carried a strong proportion of IMNM-enriched pathological signatures, notably a complement-linked 'tumour-like' inflammatory fibroblast signature and a specific interferon response, characterised by the expression of metallothioneins. Peri-necrotic areas were characterised by pathological muscle signatures carrying interferon response and FABP4+ metabolically dysfunctional signatures. In conclusion, IMNM necrotic muscle areas are linked to a specific SFRP4-expressing fibroblast subtype interacting with macrophages, potentially driving the pathological muscle phenotype and contributing to inflammation, fibro-fatty replacement, and strength loss.

title: Statistical Parametric Mapping reveals sex-specific, phase-dependent differences in bilateral three-dimensional ground reaction force during Wushu Changbing PiJi in high-level athletes.
abstract: PiJi is a core attacking technique in Wushu Changbing competition, but continuous waveform evidence remains limited regarding the sex-specific phase characteristics of bilateral 3D ground reaction force (GRF) during PiJi performed with maximal voluntary effort (MVE). This study aimed to compare continuous changes in trailing-foot, lead-foot, and net bilateral GRF between high-level male and female athletes during PiJi performed with MVE. In this cross-sectional, laboratory-based observational study, 44 right-hand-dominant athletes, including 22 male athletes and 22 female athletes, performed PiJi with MVE, yielding 616 valid trials. Bilateral 3D GRF was recorded using two force plates. Each trial was time-normalized and linearly interpolated to 143 equally spaced nodes, and within-participant mean waveforms were calculated before between-group differences were analyzed using statistical parametric mapping. Primary analyses used random-field-theory inference, with sensitivity examined using 5,000 permutation tests. After Bonferroni correction, phase-specific sex differences were detected in trailing-foot, lead-foot, and net bilateral 3D GRF. Scalar localization showed that male athletes had higher trailing-foot Fy during the middle phase (33.98%-47.04%) and higher trailing-foot Fx (62.41%-71.99%) and net bilateral Fx (54.18%-70.41%) during the middle-to-late phase; female athletes showed only a brief period of higher trailing-foot vertical Fz during the middle phase (42.11%-44.61%). Although lead-foot 3D GRF differed overall, no confirmatory difference was localized to any single scalar component. These findings indicate that sex-related GRF differences in high-level PiJi were concentrated mainly in specific horizontal-plane phases of trailing-foot and net bilateral force, whereas the lead-foot difference was identified only at the overall 3D GRF level. These results provide kinetic evidence for phase-specific assessment of PiJi technique and suggest that training monitoring and mechanistic research should consider foot, direction, and movement phase rather than relying only on peak force or discrete variables. Future studies integrating multimodal measures and sport-specific performance may further clarify the functional significance of bilateral force-generation patterns.

title: Work-related musculoskeletal disorders among civil servants attending healthcare facilities in Bangladesh: An observational cross-sectional study.
abstract: BackgroundWork-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs) are a major occupational health concern worldwide, significantly affecting employees' well-being and productivity. Government employees in Bangladesh are particularly vulnerable to WMSDs due to the sedentary or repetitive nature of their work (e.g., prolonged computer use, repetitive typing, and manual mechanical tasks).ObjectiveThis study aimed to determine the clinical distribution, patterns, and associated factors of WMSDs among government employees in Bangladesh and evaluate the subjective impact on workers' productivity and quality of life.MethodsA retrospective descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted at the Government Employees Hospital in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Participants were recruited using consecutive sampling from government employees attending the Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation Department. Descriptive and inferential statistics (Chi-square and Fisher's exact tests via R software) were used to examine the distribution of conditions like low back pain, knee osteoarthritis, cervical spondylosis, frozen shoulder. Productivity and quality of life were assessed through structured clinical interviews, while demographic characteristics, work type, and employment grade were analyzed to identify associated factors.ResultsNonspecific low back pain was the most prevalent condition (27.23%), particularly among retired employees (34.62%) and sedentary workers (26.97%). Knee osteoarthritis (10.81%) and cervical spondylosis (8.97%) were more common among older and dynamic workers. The most commonly affected sites were the lower back (43.73%), knees, shoulders, and neck. Disease patterns varied significantly by age, and government service grade.ConclusionThe high proportion of diagnosed cases among Bangladeshi government employees underscores the need for interventions including ergonomic modifications, regular health assessments, and early screening strategies to reduce WMSD impact and inform public sector health policies.

title: Sleep Management in Paralympic Sports: Knowledge, Monitoring Practices, and Perceived Barriers among Coaches and Healthcare Staff.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Coaches and healthcare staff play a crucial role in disseminating knowledge about the importance of sleep to develop a precise balance between recovery and the demands imposed by sports training.
OBJECTIVES: To assess the knowledge on sleep, jet lag, and sleep hygiene (SH) among coaches and healthcare staff in Paralympic sports; 2) to identify whether the sleep of Paralympic athletes is monitored, and which instruments are commonly used; and 3) to identify the main barriers faced in sleep management.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: The present cross-sectional study was conducted with 60 coaches and healthcare staff who work in the preparation of elite Paralympic athletes. The participants filled out the Sleep Beliefs Scale and a structured questionnaire before traveling to the 2020 Tokyo Paralympic Games.
RESULTS: Coaches and healthcare staff understand the importance of sleep for sports performance and recovery, but only 56% monitored their sleep. The most commonly used methods were subjective. Lack of adherence and commitment among Paralympic athletes (27%) and lack of training (19%) were the main barriers to sleep management.
CONCLUSION: Coaches and healthcare staff are aware of the importance of sleep; however, educational programs are needed to improve the training of coaching and healthcare staff for efficient sleep management and to raise awareness among Paralympic athletes about the importance of sleep.
